andersen-little-mermaid-1837:
Hans Christian Andersen published 'The Little Mermaid' in 1837, in his early set of tales told for children. The story, in a classic English rendering from his collected Fairy Tales, is the source of the modern mermaid tale. It is far sadder than the films that borrowed it.

The youngest daughter of the Sea King longs for the world above the waves and for a human soul. She trades her voice to a sea witch for legs, and wins the prince's love but not his hand. Refusing to kill him to save herself, she dissolves into foam, and is lifted toward a new hope. Andersen's tale turns on love, pain, and the hunger for an immortal soul.
arxiv-2512-00337:
Number theory asks which algebraic number fields admit a Euclidean algorithm for their ideal classes. Sunil Kumar Pasupulati studies Euclidean ideal classes in real biquadratic fields in 2025, from a genus-theoretic perspective. Earlier work by Lenstra reached such results only by assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.

Under that hypothesis, a field with unit rank at least one has a Euclidean ideal exactly when its class group is cyclic. Later work aims to remove the assumption in special families. Pasupulati obtains unconditional existence results via genus theory, progress toward proofs that need no unproven conjectures. Biquadratic fields, built from two square roots, are a family small enough to settle completely.
arxiv-2512-00637:
Amr Ahmadain and Ming Yang wrote a 2025 physics paper on strings moving on a cone. In string theory, a moving string sweeps out a surface called a worldsheet. They study a model of closed bosonic strings in a flat, two-dimensional cone, written in polar coordinates.

The authors compute a key quantity, the cylinder partition function, for that setup. To do the math, they first place the worldsheet on a rectangular lattice, a grid of points. Then they take the limit as the grid spacing shrinks to zero. Work like this links string motion near a sharp tip to black hole entropy, the count of a black hole's hidden states.
arxiv-2512-00737:
G Channagowdra and a large team of physicists report a new magnetic effect in a 2025 paper. They study altermagnets, a recently named class of magnets. An altermagnet has no net magnetic moment, yet it breaks a deep symmetry that mixes space reversal and time reversal.

Most altermagnets have two magnetic sites with opposite spins, linked by a rotation inside the unit cell. Using resonant inelastic X-ray scattering, the team reads each sublattice on its own through circular dichroism. They report a doubled form they call bi-altermagnetism. The finding sharpens how scientists can detect and sort these unusual magnets.
arxiv-2512-00837:
Yukang Lin and seven coauthors present WaterSearch in a 2025 paper on watermarking AI text. Watermarks hide a detectable signal inside text written by large language models. That signal helps prove where text came from, which supports accountability and trust.

Most methods steer token choices as text is generated, then detect the signal with a statistical test. Lin and coauthors take a search-based route that also weighs text quality. Their quality-aware framework looks for watermarked outputs that still read well. Balancing detection strength against readability is key if watermarks are to be used on real products.
arxiv-2512-01437:
Suhyeon Lee and Hyeongyeong Kim study a selfish mining push on Monero in 2025. Selfish mining hides found blocks to gain an edge. The Qubic pool said it ran such a push on the Monero coin network. Claims of that scale need hard proof.

The pair rebuilt Qubic-linked blocks from node and pool data. They found ten spans that fit selfish mining acts. In those spans, Qubic's share of mining power rose to a mid range. It never hit full control of the chain. Their work shows both the real reach and the clear limits of the push.
arxiv-2512-01537:
Eliya Nachmani and Tal Shuster build a new audio codec for speech and sound. Neural codecs now rebuild sound with high quality. Most squeeze sound with stacked vector codes. Those codes limit the shape of the latent space. Correlations between traits are then hard to keep.

Their codec, q2d2, uses two-dimensional quantization instead. That form keeps richer geometry in the latent space. Richer form should yield better sound at the same bit rate. Better codecs cut bandwidth for calls, streams, and stored voice data. Two-dimensional codes also ease streaming, since partial sound can be rebuilt early while later bits are still on their way.
arxiv-2512-01937:
On an energy level of a mechanical system, motion is governed by a geometric structure called an odd-symplectic form. Samanyu Sanjay's 2025 paper studies the special Zoll case, where the motion is as regular as possible: every path closes into a circle, up to a uniform change of time scale.

The question is whether Zoll forms are locally the best possible in a precise sense, systolic optimality measured in a smooth, second-order way. Systoles compare the shortest closed motion against the total volume, a classic theme in geometry. Settling the local question clarifies how rigid these perfectly periodic systems are among their neighbors.
arxiv-2512-02037:
Pairs trading bets that two assets that usually move together will return to their shared pattern after drifting apart. Marek Adamczyk's 2025 study applies deep learning to this classic statistical arbitrage strategy on the Polish equities market, with a twist on how the pair is built.

Instead of a second, highly correlated asset, Adamczyk substitutes a replication of the first asset built from so-called risk factors, chosen to mimic it as accurately as possible. Trading the gap between an asset and its synthetic twin is the strategy's engine. The study tests whether modern learning methods sharpen a well-worn idea on a smaller European market.
arxiv-2512-02137:
If the early universe changed phase, bubbles of the new state would have nucleated, grown, and collided, shaking spacetime itself. Katarina Trailović's 2025 paper studies the gravitational waves from such bubble collisions, with attention to their polarization, a property detectors may one day measure.

New physics beyond the Standard Model could drive a first-order transition in the universe's first instants, long before any light existed to observe it. Gravitational waves from the collisions would carry the news across cosmic time to future observatories. Knowing their polarization in advance helps instrument designers and analysts recognize the signal when it comes.
arxiv-2512-02237:
Young stars grow by pulling in gas from the disks around them, and the rate of that infall shapes how disks evolve and planets form. Sean Brittain and three co-authors trace in 2025 how accretion rates change as intermediate-mass stars age from T Tauri youth toward Herbig maturity.

They compare the younger intermediate-mass T Tauri stars with the older Herbig stars they become, using median accretion rates as the yardstick. How quickly accretion fades sets the clock for planet formation, since planets must assemble before the gas is gone. The evolutionary picture helps observers read a young star's age and future from its present appetite.
arxiv-2512-02737:
Tristan Amadei and co-authors locate drones from their camera view alone, without paired training data. In places where satellite navigation is denied, image based localization keeps unmanned aircraft on course. Standard methods match drone images to geo referenced satellite views.

Training those methods needs large paired drone and satellite datasets, which are costly and often unavailable. The team's self supervised approach learns from reference imagery alone. Cheaper training could bring reliable visual navigation to more regions and missions, from rescue work to inspection flights. Less gear on the ground means more flights can be run by small teams with small funds and short lead times.
arxiv-2512-03137:
Some quantum materials hide particles that carry no charge. Penghao Zhu, Archisman Panigrahi, Leonid Levitov, and Nandini Trivedi look for a way to spot them in this 2025 work. The materials are quantum spin liquids, and the hidden particles are called spinons.

Spinons do not respond to normal electric or magnetic probes, so clear signs are rare. The authors propose using strain, a gentle stretch or squeeze, as a probe. A clear strain response could reveal spinons at work. That would give labs a new tool for a long-standing puzzle in condensed matter physics. A strain probe would suit labs that can stretch samples while watching for spinon signs.
arxiv-2512-03237:
A 3D scan shows shape, but not what things are made of. Nafiseh Izadyar and Teseo Schneider tackle that gap in this 2025 work. Material traits decide how objects look, yet most shape data sets ignore them.

The authors use large language models in two stages to infer materials from point clouds. The clouds come with rough segment labels. Knowing material from shape alone could help robots grasp objects safely. It could also improve virtual scenes, where surfaces must react to light in a realistic way. Coarse segments are enough to start, which suits scans made by fast capture tools.
arxiv-2512-03337:
Who gets to write the encyclopedia is changing again. Aliakbar Mehdizadeh and Martin Hilbert study Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, in this 2025 work. A quarter century ago, Wikipedia's crowd model replaced the old expert-driven standard.

The authors ask whether AI and human encyclopedias rest on the same grounds of authority. They call the shift epistemic substitution, a swap in what counts as trusted knowledge. Their study matters as readers turn to AI text for facts. It helps frame debates on trust, authorship, and truth online. Authority shifts matter because readers rarely check who, or what, wrote an encyclopedia entry.
arxiv-2601-06637:
Abhishek Mishra and co-authors extract aspect terms with spiking neural networks in 2026. Aspect Term Extraction identifies aspect terms in review sentences automatically. It is a key subtask of sentiment analysis, they note.

Most existing approaches use energy-intensive deep neural networks for the task. They treat extraction as sequence labeling over the review text. This paper proposes a more energy-efficient alternative using spiking networks. Spiking networks fire sparsely, closer to how real neurons signal. That sparsity is where their energy savings come from in principle. The work tests whether accuracy survives the switch to spikes. Green AI readers get evidence on neuromorphic methods for language tasks. Sentiment pipelines could run cheaper if such results hold broadly.
arxiv-2601-06737:
Anay Sinhal and three co-authors solve two real scheduling tasks by shrinking them to known ones in 2026. Each task is recast as a classic task with a known fast fix. That move, called a reduction, is the heart of their whole paper.

First comes the task of beds for sick folks in a hospital ward. It shrinks to a match task, solved by flow through a graph. Next comes the task of class times at a large school. They prove that task is NP-complete, by a shrink from graph coloring. A quick greedy plan then does the job well enough in use. The pair shows both faces of hard tasks in one short paper. Beds and class times make the pure math feel close and real.
arxiv-2601-06937:
Fozle Rabbi Shafi and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers mind_call. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Anwar Hossain, Salimur Choudhury. Large Language Model (LLM)–based systems increasingly rely on function calling to enable structured and controllable interaction with external data sources.

Yet existing datasets do not address mental health–oriented access to wearable sensor data. The work presents a synthetic function-calling dataset designed for mental health assistance grounded in wearable health signals such as sleep. Physical activity, cardiovascular measures, stress indicators, and metabolic data. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07037:
Research by Koray Aydoğan and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with subspace selected variational quantum configuration interaction with a partial walsh series. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Estimating the ground-state energy of a quantum system is one of the most promising applications for quantum algorithms.

Here the authors propose a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) Ansatz for finding ground state configuration interaction (CI) wavefunctions. We map CI for fermions to a quantum circuit using a subspace superposition, then apply diagonal Walsh operators to encode the wavefunction. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07137:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Swastik Kopparty and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers recovering polynomials over finite fields from noisy character values. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Let g ( X ) g(X) be a polynomial over a finite field 𝔽 q with degree o o. And let χ be the quadratic residue character.

We give a polynomial time algorithm to recover g ( X ) g(X) (up to perfect square factors) given. The values of χ ∘ g g on 𝔽 q. With up to a constant fraction of the values having errors. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07537:
Giordano d'Alosio and colleagues present FairRF, a search method for fairer software, in a 2026 preprint. AI and machine learning systems now make decisions in sensitive areas, which raises fairness concerns. Many fixes exist, but most work as black boxes. Stakeholders cannot easily choose their own balance between fairness and prediction accuracy.

FairRF uses multi-objective search to make that trade-off visible and adjustable. It handles both single protected traits and intersectional cases, where traits combine. The goal is software fairness that teams can tune to their needs. Readers in software engineering get a method that treats fairness and effectiveness as goals to balance openly, not as a single hidden score.
arxiv-2601-07837:
Elvin Rada proposes and analyzes a new iterative scheme for fixed-point problems in generalized Banach spaces. The setting is cone b,p-normed Banach spaces, which stretch the usual notion of distance. His 2026 preprint builds a multi-inertial lambda-iteration scheme. It extends the classical Krasnoselskii-Mann method and two-step inertial iterations. Three independent inertial parameters drive the scheme, along with several error-control sequences.

Inertial terms use past steps to speed convergence, like momentum in optimization. Multiple parameters give finer control over that acceleration. Working in cone normed spaces widens the problems the method can address. Convergence analysis must then be rebuilt for the weaker distance rules. The paper serves specialists in nonlinear analysis and iterative methods. It adds a flexible scheme to a well-developed family.
arxiv-2601-07937:
Zihao Qi and Christopher Earls bring attention tools into the math of operator growth. The broad operator growth hypothesis tracks time change of operators through Lanczos coefficients. In practice, weak numeric stability and memory cost limit how many coefficients can be found with exact care. The usual path fits early coefficients to late time forms. That can miss past based structures that later shape what can be observed. Their 2026 preprint proposes attention in Krylov space.

Krylov space is the arena where Lanczos methods track an operator's growth. Attention could weigh far off coefficients by how much they count, in place of blind fits. Small structures in these numbers carry real physics about the system. To catch them would sharpen forecasts of operator spread and chaos. The paper serves scholars in quantum dynamics and many-body theory. It borrows a machine learning idea for a hard numerical problem.
arxiv-2601-08137:
Kazuhiro Seki and three co-authors show a dissipative way to prepare a quantum ground state. Their 2026 arXiv paper runs the protocol on a trapped-ion quantum computer. The test system is a quantum spin chain, a line of interacting quantum spins.

Ground states are prized starting points for quantum simulation, but they are hard to reach. The team first derives a Kraus representation of the dissipation channel. That channel follows a protocol proposed by Ding and co-authors. Dissipation here is a tool, not a flaw: it drains energy until the chain settles low. The trapped-ion run proves the idea on real hardware.
arxiv-2601-08237:
Haoran Su, Yandong Sun, and Congjia Yu argue that language models are ending manual reward engineering. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets multi-agent reinforcement learning. Hand-built reward functions remain a persistent bottleneck there, and multi-agent settings make it worse.

Credit assignment grows ambiguous when many agents act at once. Environments shift as other agents learn, and complexity scales fast with team size. The authors claim language models enable a shift from numeric rewards to natural language objectives. Stating goals in words could free designers from brittle reward tuning. Readers in agent research get a position paper on a possible new coordination paradigm.
arxiv-2601-08737:
Four authors from Brazil study a black hole of the Frolov type with a cloud of strings near it. A black hole is a place where pull is so strong that light can not leave. The Frolov type is known for a smooth core, with no sharp point at its heart. A cloud of strings is a ring of thin lines of matter.

The team works out the shape of space near this pair. They check if the core stays smooth and if known rules for energy still hold. They also track paths of light and mass near the hole, and they study heat traits of the hole. A reader in this field gets a full map of how the string cloud shifts the hole.
arxiv-2601-08837:
Nine authors, led by P. Bisconti, show a new way to slip past the guards of chat models. Guards block asks for harm. A foe can hide such an ask in a tale with a cyberpunk style. The model is then asked to break the tale down by the roles in old folk tales, such as hero and foe.

That break down task pulls the hid harm out step by step. The team calls the trick Adversarial Tales. It grows out of past work that used verse to hide harm. A reader who guards AI gets a clear case to test for. Tale form and role play can be a mask, not just a style choice.
arxiv-2601-09037:
M. Mahmudul Hasan Sajeeb and five co-authors build a chance based PC for a key task in wireless links. The task is to split mixed signals from many senders at one base. Chance PCs use bits that flip by chance to search for good picks. Real tasks need dense links between those bits, which scale poor in hard gear.

The team thins the link graph with help bits that copy a main bit. They then run a full solver on a field chip. The solver heats and cools many copies at once to dodge poor picks. A reader in gear design gets a path to chance PCs that can take real, dense tasks.
arxiv-2601-09437:
Sani Biswas presents a numerical scheme for stochastic differential equations that grow too fast for standard methods. The 2026 arXiv paper builds a randomized, tamed Milstein scheme. The equations in question have drift terms with superlinear growth and limited smoothness in time, measured by Hölder continuity.

Superlinear drift makes naive simulations blow up, so the drift must be tamed. The Milstein method adds a correction term that improves accuracy for noisy systems. Randomizing the time steps is the paper's twist for handling rough time dependence. Such schemes support simulations in finance and physics where the noise is strong and the growth is wild.
arxiv-2601-09637:
Hiroki Yoshida and Takehito Yokoyama propose a new route by which light can magnetize a material. Their 2026 arXiv paper explains the inverse Faraday and inverse Cotton-Mouton effects through quantum geometry. The key players are the quantum metric quadrupole and a weighted quantum metric.

Within a semiclassical Boltzmann transport framework, the authors build a general theory of light-induced magnetization. The response is second order in the light's electric field. Geometry-driven effects could one day let pulses of light switch magnetism at ultrafast speeds. That prospect drives interest in optical control of magnetic memory.
arxiv-2601-09737:
Fernando Alcalde Cuesta, Gustavo Guerberoff, and Álvaro Lozano Rojo time how evolution plays out on networks. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies absorption and fixation times for evolutionary processes on graphs. In these models, individuals sit on graph nodes and replace their neighbors over time.

The classic Moran process replaces one random neighbor at a step. Proliferation processes can replace several neighbors at once, with chances set by a Bernoulli or binomial draw. The authors compare updating rules by how long takeover takes. Fixation times matter in biology, where they measure how fast a trait can sweep a population.
arxiv-2601-09937:
Saber Zerhoudi and Michael Granitzer built a tool for tests of how people seek facts. Search now comes in many forms. Some tools cite web pages. Some use stored text. Some act as agents that plan steps on their own. Each form may shape the user task in a new way.

To run fair tests, labs must set up all these forms. That setup work is slow and hard. The pair made UXLab, a free web tool that hosts such tests. It cuts the setup load for labs. That lets them spend more time on the test itself and on what users do.
arxiv-2601-10437:
Jun Wang and Qiang Zhao study six rare decays of the D0 meson. A meson is a pair of a quark and its anti kin. The D0 can decay to a vector and a pseudoscalar meson. Some such decays are curbed by the Cabibbo rule. They are named singly Cabibbo suppressed.

Rates for these decays test how quarks mix and shift. The team run a joint fit of all six paths. A joint fit can show pulls that one path hides. It ties the rates to shared terms. The work aids tests of the quark mix rules that rule weak decays.
arxiv-2601-10637:
Zihao Yang, Matthias Rempel, Sarah Gibson, and Giuliana de Toma test a method that maps the Sun's corona and its magnetic field. The two-dimensional coronal seismology method uses data from the CoMP and UCoMP instruments. It reads the speed of waves across the corona from Doppler shifts. It reads gas density from the brightness ratio of two iron lines.

Together, wave speed and density give field strength, while wave paths trace field direction. The authors check this pipeline with forward modeling, building fake data from a known model corona. If the method recovers the known field, its maps of the real Sun can be trusted. Such maps feed space weather forecasts.
arxiv-2601-10737:
Giuseppe Romano, Rodrigo Arrieta, and Steven G. Johnson work on topology optimization, the art of letting math shape a part. Designs that can be built are binary: material or no material. Binary maps have no smooth slope, which clashes with gradient-based search. The subpixel-smoothed projection method eases that clash by smoothing edges below the pixel scale.

The method used a first-order expansion of the filtered field. The authors push it to second order. Higher order means finer accuracy near edges, where designs are won or lost. Better gradients let optimizers carve lighter, stronger parts. The work serves engineers who design real parts in photonics, mechanics, and beyond.
arxiv-2601-11137:
David J. Lusher and Andrea Sansica simulate turbulent transonic buffet cells on infinite swept wings. Transonic buffet is a shock-wave and boundary-layer interaction that shakes wings. In two dimensions it shows chordwise shock oscillations at low Strouhal numbers. In three it forms spanwise cells of separation and reattachment at higher ones. Airliners must stay clear of this regime.

The authors run scale-resolving simulations and add data-driven modal analysis. Scale-resolving runs capture the turbulent eddies that simpler models average away. Modal analysis then pulls out the dominant patterns of the buffet cells. Understanding the cells' rhythm and size helps designers predict buffet onset on swept wings, where most jets earn their keep.
arxiv-2601-11237:
Anthony Britto writes on time series that break a key rule in this preprint. The rule is ergodicity, which links time means to true means. When a series breaks it, forecasts and claims grow shaky. His 2026 work offers a fix based on likelihood.

The method finds transforms that restore ergodic form to a series. It is built to sit well with standard model types. Gaussian processes are one such type named in the work. ARMA and GARCH models, both stock tools, also fit the frame. The aim is a shared fix, not a trick for one model. That breadth could help analysts who meet odd series in the wild.
arxiv-2601-11337:
Elliot Lynch and Guillaume Laibe ease local models of spherical gas flows. Their 2026 preprint builds rescaling transforms for such models. A past work gave a local model of a gas cloud. The cloud could contract or expand as a sphere.

Such a model can probe turbulence and small instabilities. The new work adapts super-comoving variables to that local frame. Those variables come from studies of cosmic structure growth. Rescaling strips out the bulk growth or shrink of the cloud. What is left is the small-scale physics in clean form. Analytic solutions then come much more easily. Complex flows can be checked against the background with less pain.
arxiv-2601-11537:
The AIEP Initiative team report lessons from AI farm advice for smallholders. Their 2026 preprint covers five advisory MVPs in two countries. The services ran in Kenya and in Bihar, India. Smallholder farmers often lack timely, local agronomy advice.

AI-based advisory tools aim to close that gap at scale. The team built minimum viable products and deployed them live. An 800-farmer study found high user satisfaction in the trial. The reported net promoter score sat near 60. Technical learnings from the builds are the paper's core. They cover what worked, what failed, and what scales. Such field lessons guide the next wave of farm AI.
arxiv-2601-11937:
Fatih Maulana asks how circuit depth and qubit count trade off in quantum classifiers. The test task is to spot Higgs boson signals in crash data. Such data sets are vast and strain plain machines. Quantum learning may help, but today's quantum chips are noisy and small.

He varies depth and qubit count to see which matters more. Deep circuits can express more, yet build more noise. More qubits hold more data traits at once. The study maps that trade for one real physics task on near-term chips.  The maps help pick chip size for such search tasks.
arxiv-2601-12137:
Anzhe Cheng, Shukai Duan, Shixuan Li, and their co-authors fix two flaws in mixture-of-experts models. Such models split work among expert sub-nets to save compute. One flaw is load imbalance, where a few experts get most work in a rich-get-richer loop.

The second flaw is that experts learn near the same traits, which wastes their point. Their method, named EMoE in the work, routes work by an eigenbasis guide. Better routing could keep experts both busy and distinct. That would make large models cheaper to run well.  More even load also cuts wait time in large runs.
arxiv-2601-12237:
Sijia Ke, Yusuf Shaidu, and Jeffrey B. Neaton compute how two layers of the magnetic semiconductor CrSBr couple when twin-stacked. In layered materials, interlayer coupling can tune magnetic, electronic, and optical traits. The team use state-of-the-art first-principles calculations.

They find the coupling is highly nonlinear in twist angle. It is also nonmonotonic, with a sharp peak at the twin-stacking form. A peak at one set angle gives a knob for device design. Thin magnetic stacks could serve memory and sensor tools.  A sharp peak gives one clear angle to build for.
arxiv-2601-12537:
Stefano Bellucci and Stefania De Matteo study where the gravitino mass term comes from in supergravity. The gravitino is the spin three halves partner of the graviton in supersymmetric gravity. Its mass term has a fixed form, called the Rarita Schwinger bilinear. The pair ask what geometric structure selects that form and no other.

They work in a reduced superspace with a single fermionic direction. Inside that space, they find a minimal projector built from superspace geometry. A Berezin projection of a canonical even form then isolates the mass bilinear. They show it is the unique Lorentz invariant bilinear that fits local supersymmetry. The result ties a key term of supergravity to pure geometry.
arxiv-2601-13137:
Yuan Gao, Zhigang Liu, Xinyu Yao, Bo Chen, and Xiaobing Zhao aim to keep large language models in line on touchy topics. As such models spread, bias and drift in core values have shown up. The drift is sharpest on race, social, and state topics.

The team puts forward a frame based on matched foes. It joins three steps. First comes more pre train. Next comes teach by task prompts. Last comes foe train, where hard cases push the model to hold its line. Their goal is a model whose values stay more even across touchy fields. For firms that ship such models, the frame offers one path to more trust in frail zones.
arxiv-2601-13237:
V. A. Vladimirov sums up a key fluid theory in just four pages. The theory is the General Lagrangian Mean theory. It gives mean flow laws made to study how small waves and mean flows act on each other. That play is core to ocean and air science.

The laws are set in a frame that moves with the mean flow speed. That frame is called pseudo Lagrangian or semi Lagrangian. By brief form, the note suits staff who know fluids but not this branch. It lays out the main ideas with no extra bulk. For ocean and air teams, a short clear sum of a hard theory has real day to day worth.
arxiv-2601-13337:
I. Rafael Martinez-Hernandez and a large team set heat to metal ties in star forming zones of our galaxy. They use a sample of 225 such zones from the DESIRED-E project. Each zone has heat reads from two ions at once. One read uses ionized nitrogen lines. The next uses ionized oxygen lines.

Heat and metal share set how a zone shines and cools. With both reads in hand, the team can tie heat to metal grade with less bias. They then use those ties to map how metal grade shifts with radius in the galaxy disk. They also map shifts by angle around the core. Such maps test how the disk built its stock of heavy atoms.
arxiv-2601-13937:
Mei Han, Martin Henk, and Fei Xue generalize a new measure in the geometry of convex bodies in 2026. Packing minima were introduced in 2021 by Henk, Schymura, and Xue. They are packing counterparts to the covering minima of Kannan and Lovász. Both link a convex body with a lattice, a regular grid of points.

The team extends packing minima to all convex bodies with the origin inside. Conjectures on volume inequalities for successive minima motivated the move. Such measures help count how lattice points fit in shapes. The geometry of numbers uses them in codes, crystals, and optimization.
arxiv-2601-14237:
Roy Ferguson and Zurab Janelidze study partial linearity inside category theory in 2026. A linear category has an isomorphism between coproducts and products. Partial linearity replaces that with an isomorphism between suitable monoidal structures. Category theory studies such structures at a very general level.

Their main results are a coherence theorem and a generalization of central morphisms. The central morphism theory extends from unital categories to this partial context. Coherence theorems assure that diagrams built from the structure agree. General results like these give algebra and logic a shared language. This 2026 arXiv paper presents that study for readers in the field.
arxiv-2601-14437:
Thuan Minh Nguyen, Vu Tuan Truong, and Long Bao Le survey a fast-moving mix in this 2026 paper. Agentic AI uses large language models with autonomous reasoning, planning, and execution. Edge computing puts processing power near the devices that gather data. Unmanned aerial vehicle swarms are groups of drones that fly as one team.

Putting agentic AI inside drone swarms opens new operational possibilities. It also brings the vision of the Internet of Drones closer to reality. The paper maps how the three parts fit: smart agents, edge hardware, and the swarm. Readers get an overview of what such swarms could do and what still blocks them.
arxiv-2601-14537:
Jushin Tei, Ryo Hanai, Satoshi Fujimoto, and Takeshi Mizushima build a theory of a lab probe in this 2026 paper. Scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy with superconducting tips are widely applied to probe exotic superconductors. The tips here are s-wave superconductors. What the technique can reveal about topological superconductors remains unclear, though.

In junctions between an s-wave superconductor and a topological superconductor, the dominant tunneling process is Andreev reflection. Cooper pairs from the tip tunnel as particle-hole excitations into the surface state. The authors work out the theory of Andreev and shot noise spectroscopy for this case. Readers get predictions experimentalists can test with a real tip.
arxiv-2601-14737:
Dildar Ali, Suman Banerjee, and Rajibul Islam study billboard advertising in this 2026 paper. Billboard advertising is an effective out-of-home technique. The goal is to select a limited number of slots and play advertisement content there. The hope is that many people observe the ads. A significant number of them may then be influenced toward the brand.

The team's twist is in the title: trajectory-driven, multi-product influence maximization. Trajectories are the real travel paths of the audience, which decide who passes which board. Multi-product means several brands compete for slots at once. Readers get a placement method that follows how crowds truly move through a city.
arxiv-2601-14937:
J. J. Segura reframes spatial statistics through the lens of partial differential equations. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with geostatistics, the study of data spread over space. Classic methods set spatial links by hand, using variograms or covariance kernels on flat domains.

A newer school defines random fields through an elliptic operator instead. The inverse of that operator acts as the field's Green operator. Segura builds this operator view for bounded domains and curved surfaces. Internal interfaces get their own boundary and transmission rules, stated as part of the model itself.
arxiv-2601-15337:
Shourya Jain and Paras Chopra test whether a user's language changes the quality of a model's answers. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with fairness across languages. A user should not be worse off for the language they choose to write in.

The authors build a set of real-world, open-ended questions from the WildChat dataset. They ask the same questions across languages and grade the replies. The study checks if answer quality depends on the query language. Its title gives the thrust: models entangle language and culture, so the two are hard to pull apart.
arxiv-2601-15437:
Sohyeon Park, Jesus Armando Beltran, and co-authors probe what language models quietly assume about autism. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with chatbots such as ChatGPT, which could support autistic people. That promise depends on the models' hidden views, biases included.

Rather than prompt one model, the authors build multi-agent simulations. Autistic and non-autistic agents act out complex social scenarios together. Watching those interactions reveals the models' implicit perspectives on autism. The method goes beyond single replies to show how the hidden assumptions play out in a live, unfolding social setting today.
arxiv-2601-15737:
Hanning Zhang and five co-authors teach machines to prove physics theorems in a 2026 arXiv paper. Formal languages joined with language models have reshaped theorem proving. They give proofs a rigorous, checkable base. Math and computer science have felt that shift most. Physics has lagged, with its own notations and habits. Their system is called PhysProver. It advances automatic theorem proving for physics, per the title.

Foundation models and agentic systems keep pushing formal reasoning forward. They near the natural-language ease of plain language models. Bringing that power to physics could speed theory work. Formal checks catch gaps that informal derivations hide. The paper targets the tools gap between math proving, which is maturing, and physics proving, which is not.
arxiv-2601-16237:
Vik Pant and Eric Yu lay maths ground for teams that both join and vie. Their 2026 preprint deals with joint groups like teams and joint firms. Each part helps make a joint good. Each part also vies for fame, funds and gifts from that good. That clash breeds free ride acts, where a part takes but gives less.

Pant and Yu frame faith and joint act in code maths terms. A firm frame can show when joint work will hold or fail. It can also guide rules that keep each part true. Such rules serve real joint firms and teams. The work joins game maths to group design.
arxiv-2601-16337:
Jiguang Yu and three coauthors model how chem pull shapes growth in a mixed tumor model. Their 2026 preprint joins growth maths to ward work with path teams. The model mixes spread maths with rate maths in one frame. It holds two cell types, one frail to drugs and one firm. It also holds stroma states that can swap in time.

Chem pull draws cells and shapes where each type grows. Pull plus swap can form zones that shield firm cells. Such zones may drive drug fail in real tumors. The model lets teams test drug plans in maths first. It stems from live work with ward path staff.
arxiv-2601-16737:
Steffen Knoblauch, Ram Kumar Muthusamy, Pedram Ghamisi, and Alexander Zipf aim to find road cracks by machine. Highways wear out fast as heat swings grow harsh. Crews must fix cracks before they spread wide. That calls for sharp maps of where cracks sit. Their 2026 preprint tests free data for that task.

Open maps and free sky shots may flag crack sites. The team checks how far such free sources go. Good flags let crews send teams to the worst spots first. That saves funds and cuts road risk. The work links earth data with road care at scale.
arxiv-2601-16837:
Edoardo Otranto and Luca Scaffidi Domianello model how market swings spread and sync. Swings in one stock or index can spark swings in the next. Groups of assets oft rise and fall in shared waves. Their 2026 preprint builds a joint model for those two acts. The model treats swing size as a chain of linked steps.

Each step's size rests on past steps and peer moves. That frame can trace spill from one asset to crowds. It can also trace the shared wave that lifts all. Banks and funds need such maps for risk plans. The model adds a tool tuned to swing data as counts.
arxiv-2601-16937:
Joseph Baine and Chris Hone give a shape-based read of tilting sheaves on flag forms. Flag forms pack chains of spaces in neat steps. Tilting sheaves on them carry grade and mix traits. Their counts match a Jordan-Hölder count rule. Their 2026 preprint reads those counts as glow over dual shapes.

The dual shapes are Richardson forms in the twin flag world. Sheaves there are a motive-flavored swap for parity sheaves. This swap keeps the count proof clean and broad. Such bridges join count rules to shape facts. They aid pure work on forms tied to Lie theory.
arxiv-2601-17037:
Aahana Basappa and a team of five co-authors build a test for sight AI's blind spots. Sight-text bots read shots and write of them. Text-to-shot bots make shots from words. Both kinds fail on plain sight traits. Aim, count, and place of things trip them up. Their 2026 preprint, AMVICC, sorts those fails side by side.

The test lets teams set read fails next to make fails. Shared gaps point to deep flaws in sight sense. Such maps show what bots truly grasp of scenes. They guide fixes past mere scale-up of bots. Safe use in cars and care needs such maps.
arxiv-2601-17237:
Mike Ranzinger and six co-authors report on C-RADIOv4, a vision model for image tasks. The model learns from many teacher models at once. That method is called multi-teacher distillation. A single student model keeps the skills of each teacher. It can even improve on them in places. The design builds on the AM-RADIO and RADIOv2.5 models before it.

The report says the new model scores better on key tasks that come after training. It does so at the same compute cost as before. Such shared backbones serve many vision jobs at once. Teams can use one base for search, tagging, and more. The report tracks what changed in this release.
arxiv-2601-17337:
R. Orive and F. Wielonsky give a full analysis of a Coulomb equilibrium problem. Charges spread out until push and pull balance. The setting is Euclidean space in two or more dimensions. An outside field shapes where the charges settle. That field comes from a pair of charges, one that attracts and one that repels.

The kernel at the core falls off with distance in a set power law. The outside field is non-convex, so the balance can take odd forms. Full analysis in such cases is rare and hard. Results like this serve electrostatics and random matrix theory. They show where charge gathers when forces fight. The paired field is a clean test case with rich behavior.
arxiv-2601-17437:
Bahador Bahmani models soft biological materials with honest doubt ranges. Tissues vary a lot from person to person. Patient-specific design needs models that fit that spread. The materials are highly nonlinear. They are also stochastic by nature, due to mixed microstructure. Bahmani uses conformal quantile regression for the task.

The method gives probabilistic constitutive models. Those models state how tissue responds, with ranges that hold coverage. Surgeons and device teams can plan with real margins. A point guess alone would hide risk. This work brings sound uncertainty math to soft matter. It fits a field where each body is its own case.
arxiv-2601-17637:
Kazuhiro Takemoto tests if moral judgment in language models scales with size. Self-driving and other autonomous systems need moral choices. The Moral Machine framework poses life-death dilemmas to judge those choices. Takemoto evaluates 75 model configurations. Sizes run from 0.27 billion to 1,000 billion parameters. He measures alignment with human preferences on the dilemmas.

Predictable scaling would let builders plan for moral skill. Random scaling would warn against size-based trust. The study gives a map across a huge size range. Few studies span that full span in one design. Results can guide how labs test value-laden behavior. They also inform rules for systems that face such choices.
arxiv-2601-17737:
Chenyu Mu and co-authors present an agentic framework for long cinematic video from dialogue. Video models now make stunning clips from short prompts. Long, coherent stories from high-level ideas are still beyond them. Dialogue to film shows a semantic gap. A script must bridge idea and execution. Their framework is end-to-end and agentic, as the title states: the script is all you need.

A script gives scenes, lines, and pacing in a form models can follow. Agents can then plan shots against that spine. Long-form coherence is the prize for film and game tools. The work treats writing as the control layer for video. It may let small teams draft films at a scale once barred to them.
arxiv-2601-17937:
Anne Arzberger, Céline Offerman, Ujwal Gadiraju, Alessandro Bozzon, and Jie Yang ask who gets to label the data that aligns AI. Their 2026 preprint notes a blind spot in alignment work. Pipelines treat annotators as if they were interchangeable parts. In truth, a labeler's social position shapes how they judge text. That shaping stays hidden when labels are pooled into one ground truth.

The team introduces reflexive annotating as a probe. Crowd workers are invited to reflect on how their own position shapes their calls. The probe runs in a language model alignment setting. Its goal is a clearer view of where labels come from. Such clarity could make alignment data more honest about the values inside it.
arxiv-2601-18237:
Yu-Qi Xiao, Xiao-Gang He, Hong-Yi Niu, and Rong-Rong Zhang revisit a rare process that could reveal new physics. Their 2026 preprint deals with muon-to-electron conversion in R-parity violating supersymmetry. The process would break lepton flavor, a rule the standard model almost perfectly keeps. With massive neutrinos, the standard model rate is extremely low. That makes any seen signal a clean sign of something new. Models that violate R-parity give the process a fresh set of paths.

The authors recompute what those models predict for the conversion rate. Experiments hunting this process need sharp targets to judge their reach. The work ties a flagship experiment to a concrete theory.
arxiv-2601-18337:
Simone Scollo, Luca Galantucci, and Giorgio Krstulovic show that waves on quantum vortices can be seen in the normal part of superfluid helium. Their 2026 preprint studies Kelvin waves. These are helical waves that run along quantized vortices in the superfluid. At finite temperature, a normal fluid coexists with the superfluid. The team presents numeric evidence that the Kelvin waves show up directly in that normal component. They use a fully coupled model of superfluid turbulence, named FOUCAULT, to track the waves' spread and temperature dependence.

Seeing the waves in the normal fluid gives labs a new handle on them. Temperature decides how strong the signal is. The result links two components long modeled apart.
arxiv-2601-18537:
Linyong Gan and six colleagues aim to guess where a ship will be hours from now, not just in the next few ticks. Ship paths bend with wind, tide, and the aims of the crew. Small slips at the start grow fast as the guess runs on. Past tools tend to drift off the true path or draw paths no ship would take.

Their tool, named SKETCH, pins the guess to key points on the route. Those points act like sketch marks that hold the broad line of the trip. The fine path is then drawn to fit the marks. A held line should keep long guesses sane and close to how ships move. Port crews could use such guesses to plan berths and to spot ships that stray toward risk.
arxiv-2601-18637:
Quoc Hoan Tran and three colleagues ask if a learned quantum tool can in truth make any spread of quantum states. To learn a spread is to build a tool that can give out states drawn as if from that spread. Such tools are key if we want to study states we cannot yet make by hand. The hard ask is one of reach: can one set form be bent to fit all spreads?

That kind of reach claim is known as a claim of wide fit. The team test it for a fresh kind of state set built from steps that mix chance and choice. Their work checks if the set can fit all spreads or just a part of them. A wide fit would make the set a firm base for quantum learn tools. A short fit would map where new forms are needed.
arxiv-2601-19337:
Sayak Chowdhury and Meenakshi D'Souza blame the right part when a compound AI system fails. Modern AI systems chain several neural networks together, each doing one part of a larger task. Testing such chains for robustness and safety is hard, and current tools, black box or otherwise, fall short.

Their method, SETA, attributes faults in a statistical way across the chain's parts. Knowing which link failed, and how sure that blame is, guides fixes far better than a single fail grade. As AI systems grow into pipelines, blame assignment becomes a core engineering skill.
arxiv-2601-19737:
Erfan Bayenat and Babak Vakili model black hole evaporation with a deliberately simple system. A black hole slowly loses mass by emitting Hawking radiation. The exchange of energy between the hole and its radiation is the heart of the information problem. Their model reduces the pair to two coupled oscillators.

One oscillator stands for the geometry of the hole, the other for a radiation mode. Their free Hamiltonians carry opposite signs, a twist that mimics the hole's unusual energetics. The authors solve the coupled system analytically. The solution shows how energy sloshes between the two sectors over time. Simple models like this clarify which features of evaporation are generic and which need full gravity.
arxiv-2601-19837:
Nacereddine Sitouah, Marco Esposito, and Francesco Bruschi analyse digital identity in Europe. The eIDAS 2.0 framework sets the rules for electronic identification across the European Union. It aims at interoperability with strong, harmonised security. Its roots reach back to the first EU-wide law on electronic signatures in 1999.

The authors set self-sovereign identity against this regulatory model. Self-sovereign systems give users direct control of their identity data. The paper weighs control, privacy, and legal implications of mixing the two approaches. A European identity wallet must satisfy the law while respecting users. The analysis helps policymakers and builders see where the models clash and where they can mesh. The stakes are high for all who live and work in the bloc.
arxiv-2601-20237:
Gabor Lippner and Yujia Shi study fast, faithful transfer of a quantum state along a chain of spins. Moving a state from one end of the chain to the other is a basic task for quantum devices that pass information between parts. The authors show that near-linear-time transfer with high fidelity is achievable.

Their recipe adds loop weights at the second and the second-to-last nodes of the chain. Careful analysis of the eigenvectors gives precise estimates of transfer time and strength. Simple tweaks that make transfer both fast and reliable would help link small quantum processors into larger systems.
arxiv-2601-20637:
Panayiotis Ioannou, Pietro Liò, and Pietro Cicuta compare two tools for learning how a system moves and changes over time. One tool is the neural ordinary differential equation, a network that learns the rule of change itself. The other is symbolic regression, which searches for a plain equation that fits the data.

The team works with noisy data made by two damped systems that swing and settle. They test how far the neural models can push past the data they were trained on. They also test whether symbolic regression can find the true equations again. Their study reports three key points from the tests. The two tools serve two ends: a good forecast, or a law a scientist can read.
arxiv-2601-20737:
Si Chen and ten co-authors design AI support for learning at home. Their 2026 paper presents ParPal, a human-centred system for family learning. Family learning happens in daily routines. Children and caregivers read, practice, and build skills together at home, not just in class. Planning that learning is shared work across the family.

Most AI tutors are built for one learner or for a classroom. They miss the planning, coordination, and follow-through that home learning needs. ParPal is built for many actors at once: parents, children, and others who help. The paper shows how an AI system can support that shared planning. It speaks to families and designers who want tech that fits home life.
arxiv-2601-20837:
Ekta Patel and four co-authors ask whether two small galaxies near Andromeda once met its largest satellite. Their 2026 paper studies M33, the Triangulum galaxy. The targets are Pisces, also called LGS 3, and Andromeda XVI. Both are present-day satellites of M31, the Andromeda galaxy. The team checks if their paths once crossed M33.

Theory predicts a handful of satellites should orbit M33. Yet few have been found and confirmed, despite M33's high mass. Close past encounters could help explain where those satellites went. A meeting can strip a small galaxy or fling it away. The study uses such encounters as a clue to a past group accretion. Its results bear on how big galaxies gather their families of dwarfs.
arxiv-2601-20937:
Protection of Unconventional Superconductivity from Disorder is the subject of Sofie Castro Holbæk and three co-authors in this 2026 paper. Unconventional superconductors are prized for their high transition temperatures. Their order parameter changes sign, unlike the classic case. That sign change makes their condensates fragile to disorder. Disorder is inevitable in real materials. The tension between promise and fragility drives the study.

A superconductor that breaks under slight mess is hard to use. The authors ask how such states can be protected. Understanding protection could guide the search for hardier materials. It could also explain why some samples survive better than theory expects. The paper is a theory study of a practical worry. It speaks to materials scientists who need superconductors that work outside perfect crystals.
arxiv-2601-21337:
The Qwen Team presents a family of speech recognition models built for wide real-world use. The family has two main models of different sizes. Both can tell which language is being spoken and transcribe speech across a broad list of languages and dialects.

A third model aligns spoken words to text without generating word by word, which makes it fast and precise. The systems draw on large-scale speech training data. They also build on the strong audio skills of the team's base model. Such tools support captions, voice control, and records of meetings in many languages at once.
arxiv-2601-21937:
A benchmark described in this 2026 preprint asks a sharp question: can language models reason over scientific information that is genuinely new to them? Models score well on existing tests, but it is unclear how much of that is reasoning and how much is memory. Most evaluations score whole retrieval pipelines at once.

That design confounds reasoning with retrieval skill and tool choices, and scores are further polluted by memorized material and the shifting open web. The Retrieval-Infused Reasoning Sandbox instead separates retrieval from reasoning so each can be measured alone. Clean separation matters because a model that merely recalls cannot be trusted with the novel findings that real research produces every day.
arxiv-2601-22037:
Sami Abuzakuk and co-authors try to cut the cost of agentic workflows. Agentic systems let a language model reason, plan, and call tools to solve hard tasks. In practice they need many rounds of reasoning and tool calls, which drives up expense, delay, and failures from hallucination.

Their 2026 preprint optimizes such workflows using meta-tools, tools that act on the workflow itself rather than the task. Streamlining the steps an agent takes can reduce wasted calls and dead ends. The economics matter here. Agentic products bill by the token and the call. A leaner workflow can be the difference between a demo and a service that runs all day.
arxiv-2601-22137:
Shenghao Yang and co-authors accelerate the matrix computations inside neural network training. Matrix functions such as square roots, inverse roots. And orthogonalization sit at the heart of preconditioned gradient methods, the optimizers that reshape gradients for faster learning. Iterative algorithms compute them using mostly matrix multiplications, which suits graphics processors.

The team's 2026 preprint presents PRISM, a distribution-free adaptive method for computing these matrix functions. Adaptive computation spends effort where the numbers demand it, rather than running a fixed schedule. Faster, stabler matrix functions would speed the training of large models that rely on advanced optimizers, cutting both time and energy per experiment.
arxiv-2601-22237:
Miqaela Weller and co-authors take spectra of some of the most metal-poor gas clouds known. Their paper belongs to a project using the Large Binocular Telescope. The project aims to pin down the primordial helium abundance. That is the fraction of helium forged in the Big Bang. Nebulae poor in metals preserve that early composition best.

Accurate abundances hinge on measuring the gas density and temperature of each nebula. This installment presents spectra from the LUCI instrument of metal-poor nebulae, building the physical measurements the helium determination needs. Their 2026 preprint is one careful step in a long chain. Primordial helium is a direct test of Big Bang nucleosynthesis. That is the theory of how the first elements formed.
arxiv-2601-22337:
Aidan Bennett, Curtis Bright, Paul Colinot, and Ashwin Nayak study number strings with a rare, clean trait. A string is called perfect when its overlap with a shifted copy of itself drops to zero. Their 2026 preprint works with quaternions, a four-part number system used for spins and turns.

They show these strings match, one for one, the binary strings in a classic build of Hadamard matrices. Those matrices, with rows at right angles, serve codes and signal design. The link gives each field a new tool from the other. It may yield fresh matrices and fresh strings alike.
arxiv-2601-22937:
Andrea P. Sanna tests whether cosmic structure can form without dark matter or dark energy. The setting is a Brans–Dicke scalar-tensor theory, a modified form of gravity with an extra field. In this universe, only ordinary baryonic matter exists, so gravity alone must do the extra work.

Using linear perturbation theory, the study tracks how small clumps grow into the large-scale web of galaxies. If modified gravity can grow the right structures, it stays a live rival to dark matter. If it cannot, the test helps rule it out cleanly.

carlyle-french-revolution-vol-1-1837:
Thomas Carlyle published The French Revolution, Volume 1, in 1837, covering the fall of the Bastille. Carlyle tells the story of 1789 as epic prose poetry. Crowds, kings, and orators move in scenes of fire and chaos. The taking of the Bastille on July 14 stands at the center.

Carlyle scorns dry record and writes history as moral drama. His research was vast, yet his voice is that of a prophet, not a clerk. The book became the most influential English account of the Revolution. Dickens drew on it for A Tale of Two Cities. Volume 1 ends with the old order broken.
carlyle-french-revolution-vol-2-1837:

France tries to build a new order by law and reason. Festivals, debates, and the king's flight to Varennes mark the phase.

Carlyle shows hope curdling as factions harden and hunger persists. His prose rolls in long, heated sentences full of biblical echoes. The volume ends with the monarchy falling and war beginning. Critics praise the narrative art at full power here. Together with its companions, the work remade how English readers saw 1789.
carlyle-french-revolution-vol-3-1837:
Thomas Carlyle completed The French Revolution with Volume 3 in 1837, subtitled The Guillotine. The narrative covers the Terror, the fall of the Girondins, and the rise and fall of Robespierre. Executions mount as the Revolution devours its own children. Thermidor at last ends the Terror's worst phase.

Carlyle treats these years as moral drama on a national scale. He neither excuses the terror nor honors the old regime. The guillotine becomes the grim symbol of justice turned to vengeance. The three volumes together form one vast prose epic. They secured Carlyle's fame and still reward brave readers.

H. T. Colebrooke opened Indian studies to Britain, and his Miscellaneous Essays of 1837 gather the founding papers of the field. Volume I ranges widely over the Vedas, Sanskrit grammar, Hindu law, and astronomy in turn. Colebrooke learned Sanskrit while serving in India and wrote with an accuracy that set the field's standard for a century.

Each essay settled some question scholars had only guessed at before: the age of texts, the shape of law, the reach of Indian astronomy. Together they form the charter collection of British Indology, the shelf where the subject begins. Later researchers built on Colebrooke's groundwork in nearly every branch of the subject he touched.

His essays on Hindu algebra and on the philosophies of India carried whole fields into English for the first time. Read with the first volume, the set shows one scholar mapping a civilization's learning almost alone, essay by essay. The two volumes together remain the foundation shelf of British Indology today.
