Team activities share a credit problem: everyone agrees some players star, but measuring each person's contribution fairly is hard. The authors used soccer as a test bed, analyzing play from the European Cup 2008 tournament.

They built a network method that follows how the ball moves between players and how those passing patterns create scoring chances. From that flow they derived numbers for each player's contribution and for the team's overall performance. Duch and colleagues show that a player's value can be read from the structure of play, not just goals and assists. Their framework is meant to travel beyond soccer, to any team work where credit is disputed.
plos-pone-0011037:
Peter Sokolowski, Francis Saison, Warwick Giles and co-authors published this pregnancy study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The tension in the uterine wall is thought to help trigger labor, but it had never been charted across a whole pregnancy. The authors followed hundreds of women at an Australian hospital from their first antenatal visit to delivery.

Serial ultrasounds measured the womb's wall thickness and dimensions, and combining them with published pressure data let the team compute wall tension trajectories for each woman. They compared singleton pregnancies ending in preterm or term labor with twin pregnancies, where the wall is stretched further. Sokolowski and colleagues give obstetrics a physical curve to set against the mystery of labor timing. If tension thresholds exist, measuring them could one day flag preterm risk early.
plos-pone-0011137:
Amon, Law, Fitzgibbon and colleagues searched for ovarian cancer markers in PLOS ONE in 2010. This cancer is often found late, when cure is hard. The team compared proteins in blood and in belly fluid from women with and without the disease.

Some proteins rose in the blood of women with ovarian cancer, marking them as candidates for early tests. A blood test that flags the disease sooner could save many lives. The candidates still need checks in larger groups before clinic use. Still, pairing two fluid sources gave the search a stronger starting list.
plos-pone-0011237:
Young, Adetifa, Ota and colleagues tracked TB immune cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. During active tuberculosis, some T cells can attack the germ on several fronts at once. The team measured those versatile cells in patients during illness and again after treatment ended.

Versatile responses expanded during disease and shrank back once treatment succeeded. That pattern makes these cells a sign of current disease activity. Vaccine designers hope to build responses like these in advance. Tracking them gives trials a yardstick for judging whether a vaccine creates the right kind of immunity.
plos-pone-0011337:
Kirill Sergueev and colleagues described in 2010 a faster way to detect the plague germ, Yersinia pestis. Plague still occurs in parts of the world, and it can kill quickly, so a fast and sure test matters for treatment and for public safety. Older tests based on viruses that attack the germ were sure but often slow.

Their method lets those germ-attacking viruses multiply in a sample, then tracks the growth with a sensitive DNA test in real time. More virus growth means the plague germ was present, and the signal appears much sooner than in older assays. A rapid test that stays specific helps clinics confirm cases early. It also gives health officials a stronger tool if plague ever appears as a deliberate threat.
plos-pone-0011437:
Amanda Maestre and co-authors examined in 2010 how a blood-group gene shapes immunity to the malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax. The parasite invades red blood cells through the Duffy receptor, and people who lack that receptor resist this route of infection. Most people carry one of several forms of the receptor, and forms differ across world regions.

The team found that a person's Duffy genotype influences the antibody response they build after vivax infection. Two people with the same exposure can therefore end with different levels of immune protection, set partly by their genes. Vaccines against vivax malaria must work across those genetic differences, or they will protect some populations better than others. The study links a classic blood-group story to a practical problem in vaccine design.
plos-pone-0011537:
Anne Berry and co-authors tested in 2010 whether training the senses can sharpen memory in older adults. Working memory, holding a phone number or a plan in mind, erodes with age and limits independence. Perceptual training, practicing fine sensory distinctions such as telling similar tones or textures apart, exercises basic brain processing that memory may draw on.

The study asks whether gains from that low-level practice spill over into working memory, a transfer that brain training often promises and rarely proves. Testing transfer honestly matters, because older adults spend real money and hope on training programs. If perception practice does lift memory, it offers a gentle, drug-free support for aging minds. If it does not, the paper still serves readers by marking the boundary of what such training can do.
plos-pone-0011637:
Eric Nilsson and co-authors mapped gene networks that build the ovary's earliest follicles, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Primordial follicles hold a female's lifetime supply of eggs, held paused in development from before birth. How this founding pool forms is central to understanding fertility and its loss.

Using a systems approach, the team tracked gene activity as follicles develop and charted the regulatory networks involved. Their network analysis highlights control genes that coordinate the process. The map gives fertility researchers concrete candidates for explaining early ovarian failure and for protecting the egg supply.
plos-pone-0011737:
Daniel Kellett and co-authors studied how the cerebellum stores learned responses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The cerebellum is best known for balance and smooth movement, but some kinds of learning depend on it too, such as the trained eyeblink response in rabbits. Briefly switching off parts of its circuit had begun to split the roles of its outer cortex and its deep nuclei.

The team looked at how memories settle in the cerebellar cortex over time. Their work tests whether the cortex itself holds the lasting trace or hands it on. The answer adds a memory-filing role to the little brain's known work in movement.
plos-pone-0011837:
Wen Chih Chiang and co-authors described in 2010 an effort to deliver proteins straight to podocytes, the cells that form the kidney's main filter. Podocytes wrap around tiny blood vessels in the kidney and keep needed protein from leaking into urine. Their position exposes them to blood and urine alike, which makes them reachable in principle but hard to target in practice.

The team set up delivery systems designed to carry protein cargo to these filter cells. Reaching podocytes directly matters because damage to them drives many kidney diseases, yet general drugs wash over the whole body. A working delivery route would let future treatments act at the filter itself, where the injury actually happens.
plos-pone-0011937:
Sarah Read and co-workers tested in 2010 whether an arthritis drug could calm the immune overdrive seen in HIV infection. Even when HIV is controlled, constant immune activation helps drive the disease. Leflunomide, a drug that tempers immune cell growth, was a candidate for lowering that activation.

In a randomized study of HIV-1 infected participants, the team measured how the drug affected T cell cycling and activation. Slowing the churn of T cells could, in principle, reduce the damage activation causes over years. The trial gives an early read on whether repurposing an existing immune drug is a safe and sensible path in HIV care.
plos-pone-0012037:
Aurelia Santoro and colleagues brought in 2010 fresh proof that a small branch on the family tree of our cell power plants bears on the risk of Alzheimer's disease. The disease is the most common cause of dementia in old age. Since the power plants, the mitochondria, make the cell's energy and were thought to falter in this disease, changes in their own DNA are a clear place to look.

The branch in point is a subgroup called H5, passed down the mother's line from child to child. People who carry it were found more prone to the late form of the disease, the kind that starts in old age. A sign passed down the mother's side fits the known trend for risk to track the mother's health. It also makes the case that weak energy supply is part of the disease, not just a side show.
plos-pone-0012137:
Saravanan Thangamani, Stephen Higgs, Sarah Ziegler, and co-authors compared two ways of catching chikungunya virus in PLOS ONE in 2010. In nature this virus arrives by mosquito bite, along with mosquito saliva that tampers with the skin's defenses. Lab studies usually inject virus with a needle instead, which skips that whole first act of a real infection.

The team's work shows the immune response differs when the virus comes by mosquito rather than needle. Early events at the bite site shape how the illness unfolds, so the delivery route is part of the disease itself. That lesson affects how vaccines and treatments for mosquito-borne viruses should be tested before anyone trusts the results.
plos-pone-0012237:
Suzanne Kalb, Consuelo Garcia-Rodriguez, Jianlong Lou, and co-authors built a catcher's mitt for botulinum toxins, in PLOS ONE in 2010. These toxins are among the most potent poisons known; the sickness they cause can paralyze breathing and demand weeks of intensive care. There are several types, and the best treatment, an antitoxin matched to the type, works only when given early, so fast typing is critical.

One engineered antibody they made grabs all four major types at once, feeding them into a mass-spectrometer test that tells them apart. A single capture step for every type shortens the race to the right antitoxin. In a food poisoning outbreak or an attack, those saved hours are the point.
plos-pone-0012337:
Brendan Flynn, Amit Bhole, Nima Saeidi, and co-authors showed that stretch protects collagen from being eaten away, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Collagen is the body's main structural protein, filling bone, tendon, skin, and cornea, and enzymes that cut it allow tissues to be remodeled or, in disease, destroyed. The team had earlier proposed that the fibrils resist cutting better when under load.

Testing rebuilt collagen fibrils under mechanical strain, they found the strain indeed stabilizes them against a mammalian collagen-cutting enzyme. That coupling of force and chemistry explains how tendons can bear load for decades while remodeling slowly. It also suggests diseased tissues may lose collagen partly because their mechanics changed first.
plos-pone-0012437:
Henrique Santos, Juliano Cury, Flavia Carmo and colleagues read DNA from mangrove mud to detect oil pollution, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Tiny eukaryotes — single-celled life with a nucleus — respond quickly to contamination, making them good pollution alarms. Naming them by microscope is slow and often fails, so the team used the 18S gene as a DNA barcode instead.

Certain microbe DNA patterns lined up with oil in the sediment, marking them as indicators of contamination. Mangroves shelter coasts and nurseries for fish, yet sit near ports and oil work. A DNA test for hidden oil gives managers an early warning before damage shows in trees and wildlife.
plos-pone-0012537:
Toru Hosoi, Shota Yokoyama, Suguru Matsuo and colleagues removed an immune adaptor protein in mice and watched metabolism, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. MyD88 relays signals from many innate immune sensors, and immune pathways are increasingly tied to obesity-linked diabetes. Removing a relay this central might have protected the mice — or, as it turned out, done the opposite.

Mice lacking MyD88 faced a higher risk of diabetes in the study's setting. The result warns that gut and immune sensing also serve healthy metabolism, not only defense. Blanket suppression of innate immunity could backfire in metabolic disease, a caution for drug design.
plos-pone-0012637:
Nalam, Ahmed, Devi and co-authors compared the genetics of disease-causing Leptospira bacteria from around the world. Leptospirosis spreads from animals to people, often through water, and can be severe. Outbreak teams struggle because telling one strain from another has been unreliable.

Their 2010 study used a large global collection to map how strains relate to each other. Clear family links let health workers trace an outbreak to its source and follow its spread. Better strain naming also helps labs in different countries share results that actually match, and it sharpens vaccine and test design.
plos-pone-0012737:
Spade, Griffitt, Liu and co-authors reported that male queen conch near shore lose their fertility each breeding season. Offshore conch in the Florida Keys breed well, while nearshore animals do not. Their 2010 study examined testes of conch from both settings across the reproductive season.

Nearshore males showed testis regression just when breeding should peak. That local failure helps explain why nearshore conch numbers stay low despite fishing rules. The cause may lie in nearshore water conditions, a lead for reef and fishery managers.  Conch are a valued food and export across the Caribbean region.
plos-pone-0012837:
Fuller, Ross, Szewczyk and co-authors challenged the idea that bone itself must switch on the cells that eat bone. Osteoclasts resorb bone, and some signal from bone was thought to trigger that behaviour. Lab work had shown that blocking a certain receptor on these cells stops resorption, hinting at the trigger.

Their 2010 study found osteoclasts can be activated without bone present at all. That shifts the search for the trigger toward the cells and signals around bone. The result matters for diseases of bone loss, including osteoporosis.  The cells were grown and tested away from bone surfaces.
plos-pone-0331937:
Wenlong Jin and colleagues describe a way to build three-dimensional models of underground rock that leans on expert judgement, not just raw data. Purely data-driven models can miss twisted structures. So the team fed borehole records and survey profiles from a tantalum and niobium mining district in Jiangxi, China, into modelling software. Meanwhile, geologists added rules drawn from their own knowledge of the area.

The rebuilt model placed the richest ore where a sodium-rich granite meets the rocks above and below it, matching what miners see. Guided by those contact zones, the team picked out two promising deep targets for future drilling. They argue that mixing expert rules with data gives models that are both faster to build and closer to the real ground.
plos-pone-0333337:
Peter Okello Oyoo, Simon Okwera, Daniel Micheal Okello, and Basil Mugonola measured how efficiently 191 smallholder dairy households in northern Uganda turn inputs into profit. They compared three ways of keeping cattle: confined zero-grazing, tethering, and open herding. Their 2026 survey analysis fitted a profit frontier model. The model separates bad luck from genuine inefficiency and asks what drives each.

The drivers differed sharply by system. Herd size lifted profits under zero-grazing, while feed costs crushed them. Land helped tethered herds yet hurt herding systems. Education, improved breeds, and closeness to markets cut inefficiency almost everywhere. The model blamed over nine tenths of profit variation on inefficiency rather than chance. Management, not luck, is the main lever.
plos-pone-0340237:
Clara Punzi and four colleagues profile Italy's platform workers in this 2026 study. Gig work through apps is often pictured as a young person's stopgap. The authors test that picture with official survey data from 2018 and 2021. Machine learning models sorted out which traits predict platform work. Explainable AI tools then showed how the models reached their answers.

Platform work in Italy turned out layered and uneven. It mirrors the country's older labour market fractures and regional gaps. Financial vulnerability clustered not among the youngest workers, but among older, established ones. Many had hit job instability, underemployment, or shrinking income from regular work. Platform jobs carried the insecurity typical of non-standard employment. The findings argue against one-size-fits-all gig policy, since the workforce is really several workforces sharing an app.
plos-pone-0342637:
Mary Jewell and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study comparing two ways of finding COVID-19 clusters in Utah: traditional case interviews and genetic sequencing of virus samples. Sequencing can reveal which cases are truly linked, but health departments lacked guidance on using it during a live response. The team compared the populations each method reached and tested ways of grouping cases by their genetic similarity.

Sequencing coverage was uneven, with several non-White patient groups less likely to be sequenced at all. Genetic clusters often disagreed with interview-based ones, and many large interview clusters turned out to mix several separate virus introductions. The authors conclude that genomic data sharpens cluster definitions considerably, provided sampling is broad and cases in suspected clusters are sequenced first.
plos-pone-0344537:
Zahra Sheikhi Darani and Monireh Hosseini propose a new layer for recommendation engines in this 2026 PLOS ONE computing paper. Recommenders in social apps usually balance relevance against a fixed idea of novelty, but what feels new depends on what a person's friends have been seeing and doing.

Their framework scores each item's novelty for each user from social community behavior, and learns how much novelty that user personally likes, resolving the tug-of-war with relevance individually. Bolted onto existing engines as a post-processing step, it lifted diversity, coverage, and novelty on two real datasets, Epinions and LastFM, without sacrificing relevance. The design suits any platform where friends shape taste.
plos-pone-0344737:
Rumford and colleagues, in a 2026 study, watch the eye of a baby zebrafish rebuild itself after light-sensing cells are destroyed. Zebrafish regrow retinal cells that mammals cannot, and immune cells called microglia were suspected of guiding that repair. The team compared normal larvae with mutants bred to lack microglia, after wiping out their cone cells.

Repair proceeded surprisingly well without microglia. Support cells still woke up, multiplied, and produced new cones at much the usual pace, and inflammation-linked genes changed only modestly. A wrinkle appeared, though: a stand-in population of immune cells showed up in the mutants after damage. It rose and fell on a similar schedule, but was much scarcer and carried different surface marks. Because something filled the vacant role, the authors say they cannot cleanly credit or clear microglia. The stand-ins themselves are now a question worth chasing.
plos-pone-0345137:
Hasan Yalim Akin, Gule Cinar, and co-authors asked whether two ancient layers of the immune system interact to decide who gets sick with COVID-19. One layer is a family of natural killer cell receptors, and the other is a set of antiviral genes inherited from Neanderthals. Their 2026 study genotyped one hundred seventy-five unvaccinated patients, spanning no symptoms to severe disease, across several immune genes.

Missing both a protective receptor pattern and the Neanderthal gene variants together predicted symptoms and severe disease far better than either alone, with overall classification accuracy in the high seventies. Age, male sex, and two other gene variants added risk, while one blood group and one gene form protected. The authors present the synergy as a first, needing confirmation in larger and more diverse groups.
plos-pone-0346837:
Gornsawun and colleagues checked a bedside test for an enzyme lack in newborns along the Thai-Myanmar border in a 2026 study. Babies lacking the enzyme can develop dangerous yellowing of the skin and brain harm. Seventy-five babies, grouped by routine cord blood results, were followed with blood tests through their first four months.

The study compared cord blood with later heel-prick samples to see if both give the same answer. It also tracked how enzyme activity changes as babies grow, which affects cutoff choices. Reliable bedside testing matters in remote clinics without full labs, where early warning prevents severe jaundice.
plos-pone-0346937:
Runa Sawayama and Hajime Nobuhara asked if a drone's look can change how folk fly it. They used a phone-like screen trick to drape new looks on the same drone. A large group flew the drone with and sans the trick. The team logged each flight and asked for views in forms.

The looks did not change how much the group worked the sticks. But views of the drone swung a lot. Folk judged its age, its beast-like feel, and its sex in new ways. They even sized up its bulk and heft in fresh ways. The team says looks could help drones win a warm place in daily life.
plos-pone-0347537:
Zhao Wen and colleagues simulated what happens when individual fibres are pulled out of concrete, a small event that decides how well fibre-reinforced concrete resists cracking. Builders commonly mix in basalt or polypropylene fibres, but testing every combination in the lab is slow. Their 2026 study built a computer model combining a phase-field description of damage with a model of the glue-like bond between fibre and cement.

The predicted pull-out forces matched published experiments well. Deeper embedding and thicker fibres raised the peak load for both fibre types, and stronger bonding or a stronger cement matrix improved reinforcement further. The validated model lets engineers screen fibre choices virtually before pouring real concrete.
plos-pone-0347737:
Shijie Zhang and co-workers work on calming vibration in the drivetrain of a large wind turbine. Shaking in gears and shafts wears parts out and cuts efficiency. Their 2026 study models the linked mechanical and electrical system of a big turbine and designs a control scheme on the generator side that narrows the gap between mechanical and electrical torque.

The control also trims unwanted ripples in generator current and magnetic pull. In the model, sideways shaking in key gear parts fell, and tracking of shaft speed grew sharper. Smoother running means less wear and steadier power from each gust. The approach offers turbine makers a software route to longer-lasting machines.
plos-pone-0348137:
Jaeyoung Huh and colleagues teach an artificial intelligence system to upgrade liver ultrasound images from old machines, in this 2026 PLOS ONE imaging paper. Ultrasound is the first test for liver disease worldwide, but aging scanners produce murky pictures that can hide tumors and mislead diagnosis.

Their network learned without paired examples, using images from a twelve-year-old device as input and from a four-year-old device as the quality target, translating between the two styles. Two experienced reviewers judged the enhanced images better. If the gains hold in clinic, hospitals could stretch the useful life of older scanners, a real concern where new equipment budgets are thin.
plos-pone-0348437:
Björn Högberg and Cristian Bortes asked if stress in class spreads from teen to teen. They used data on Swedish teens, first at age thirteen, then at age sixteen. Then they ran the sums in a huge range of ways. The count of model runs topped nine thousand. Each run changed a choice such as the test type or the stress gauge.

Most runs found a spread, but a weak one. The size of the spread swung a lot, and at times it flipped sign. Few runs cleared the bar for trust. The team says stress in school comes more from the school itself than from friends. Fix the real loads first, they urge.
plos-pone-0348537:
RETRACTION: The PLOS One Editors have withdrawn a study of new fluorine-rich drugs. The study claimed these drugs could fight tumours that grow with little oxygen. After it came out, readers flagged faults in its data files. Some chart traces looked far too much alike for drugs said to be distinct. The stated tests also did not match the work.

The editors then checked the raw files the authors sent. Key claims in the text were not backed by those files. Bars on key charts did not match the raw data either. One author replied but took no stand on the choice. With the results in doubt, the journal pulled the study in full.
plos-pone-0348737: Wagner and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on brown trout swimming downstream. The fish faced water that speeds up and flows at high rates. The team paid close attention to how the trout moved, not just where they ended up. The findings matter for fish passage design at dams and weirs, where fast water can block or harm migrating fish.
plos-pone-0349237:
Yaojun Zhang, Changqiang Shen, and Ying Xiong improved a computer vision model for spotting rice diseases in 2026. Finding and locating disease early protects harvests, yet field images are cluttered, lesions are small, and heavy models run slowly.

Their model swaps in a light backbone that reads fine detail cheaply, uses an upsampling step that keeps detail, and adds flexible convolution in the neck. Against the base model it gained a little accuracy, ran notably faster, and cut computing cost and size greatly. A lighter, quicker detector is what drones and farm phones can realistically carry.
plos-pone-0349437:
Narayani Paudel Ghimire and colleagues piloted Forum Play, a form of participatory theatre, to promote respectful maternity care in urban Nepal in 2026. Mistreatment during facility births is widely reported there, and training rarely lets staff rehearse kinder behaviour.

Doctors and nurses in two large hospitals took part, with one group acting out scenes of oppression drawn from their own work and stepping in to change them. Surveys before and after compared their reported views and behaviour with a control group. Theatre based practice offers a low cost way to shift ward culture, and this pilot tests whether it moves real attitudes.
plos-pone-0349937:
Xiaobo Xu and seven colleagues dissect a grain toxin's dangers entirely on the computer. Their 2026 case study is zearalenone, an estrogen-like contaminant made by Fusarium fungi in cereals. It threatens food safety worldwide. The team combined network toxicology with molecular docking and dynamics simulations. Instead of dosing animals, they predicted which human proteins the toxin grips. Kidney damage was the hypothesised harm under the microscope.

Five core targets emerged, including well-known signalling and cancer-related proteins. The affected routes touch immune injury, inflammation, cell death, and genetic mutation. Docking and simulation both showed the toxin binding its targets snugly. Pathways famous in cancer biology appeared among the hits. The authors present the pipeline itself as a deliverable. Fast, animal-free toxicity screening could triage the thousands of food contaminants regulators face, reserving slow laboratory proof for the likeliest threats.
plos-pone-0350337:
Margaret Fletcher and co-authors follow in 2026 children with attention and hyperactivity disorder in a large United States development study, asking what shapes how they fare over five years. Children reported on family conflict, kind behaviour, and school life, while records tracked medicine use and social conditions. Growth modelling sorted children into paths such as resilient, declining, or slowly improving.

Medicine patterns linked only weakly to which path a child followed, though one non stimulant type tied to poorer outcomes. Social and structural factors mattered far more, above all ethnic discrimination, plus sex, insurance, and parents' work and partnership. Support should address context, the authors argue.
plos-pone-0350637:
Jung-Bin Park and co-authors built a deep learning tool in 2026 to warn of brain complications after surgery for Moyamoya disease in children. The rare condition narrows brain arteries, and surgery to improve blood flow can still be followed by strokes or bleeds.

The team turned blood pressure waves recorded during surgery into images and trained several image networks on them, testing on a later group of patients kept aside. Heat maps showed which wave features drove each call. A warning drawn from signals already collected could help teams watch the riskiest children more closely after surgery.
plos-pone-0350737:
Sudip Saha and colleagues designed a defense for the computer systems that watch networks for intruders. Such detectors use deep learning, but attackers can fool them with tiny, carefully crafted changes to data. Their 2026 study tested a hybrid design that mixes normal training with attack training and adds guidance drawn from what the model gets wrong.

Tested on data covering spying probes, shellcode, and worms, the system stayed accurate on clean traffic and held up far better under two common attack methods than standard neural networks. It beat the comparison models by a clear margin and also made fewer overconfident mistakes. The work matters for hospitals, banks, and factories, where a fooled detector can open the door to real damage.
plos-pone-0350837:
Lana Zuriegat and colleagues reviewed two hundred and thirty four patients with diabetic foot infections at a large hospital in Jordan. Foot infections drive long stays and amputations in diabetes. Culture results, drug resistance, first drug choices, and stay length were charted. Therapy counted as right only when a drug given in the first two days covered every germ found at the right dose and route.

Staph germs caused half of infections, and two thirds of germs resisted multiple drugs. First therapy was right in under half of cases. Yet only infection severity, not resistance or wrong first therapy, clearly predicted longer stays in adjusted models. Severity triage and faster culture guided switches matter most, the data suggest.
plos-pone-0351137:
Sepsis, the body's overwhelming response to infection, fills intensive care units in Tanzania, and Atala Jongo and colleagues tracked adults with the condition at a national referral hospital. Their 2026 PLOS One study followed patients over six months in 2023, screening everyone admitted to the unit.

About two hundred fifty patients were screened, with sepsis defined by organ failure scores within the first day. The team recorded how common sepsis was, how many patients died, and which traits predicted death. Referral hospitals receive the sickest patients from wide regions, so their numbers show the burden at its heaviest and where resources matter most.
plos-pone-0351337:
Valuable uranium sits in sandstone along the southern Junggar Basin in China. Qing Wang and colleagues studied drill cores from the Louzhuangzi area. They wanted to learn why the metal gathered there. Their work combined field mapping with microscope studies. Chemical probes examined the rock in fine detail. The paper appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

Ancient rivers built the rock formation in two layers. Winding rivers laid down the upper layer. Braided rivers built the lower layer. The lower sands let fluids pass easily. Uranium-rich ore sits mostly in that lower layer. Moving fluids later changed the rock and dropped their uranium load. Explorers can now aim drill holes more wisely.
plos-pone-0351437:
Viet-Linh Nguyen and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study of parasites in free-roaming cats caught through a trap-neuter-return program in New York City. Samples from eighty-seven cats, collected in spring and summer 2023, were tested for gut parasites, blood parasites, and exposure to Toxoplasma. Urban cats can carry organisms that also infect people, yet city-level data were scarce.

More than half the cats carried at least one parasite, most commonly the roundworm Toxocara, found in over half. Young male cats were the heaviest shedders of roundworm eggs, marking them as key drivers of contamination in shared spaces. About one in eleven cats showed antibodies to Toxoplasma. The authors recommend folding disease surveillance into neutering programs to watch risks for both cats and people.
plos-pone-0351537:
Yuemei Li authored this 2026 PLOS One modeling paper on how rock slowly deforms under load when it is also hot, a problem for deep underground engineering. Older creep models often ignore how heat damage builds over time and describe the final, accelerating stage of deformation poorly. Li combines damage mechanics with fractional calculus to build a model in which heat and stress damage grow together over time.

Checked against laboratory creep tests run at four temperatures from room level up to one hundred degrees Celsius, the model's curves matched the measured behavior closely through all three creep stages. It also captured the turning point into accelerated creep better than the classic model it improves on. The author offers it as theoretical support for judging the long-term stability of hot, deep rock projects.
plos-pone-0351637:
Yuta Nakaniida and colleagues asked whether the softness of the eye's front window relates to blood flow at the back of the eye. They measured one hundred healthy eyes with an air-puff device that films the cornea bending, and with a laser method that estimates flow in the optic nerve head. Eye length, corneal thickness, and pressure were recorded too, since each can sway the readings.

Eyes whose corneas bent more under the puff tended to have slower measured flow in the nerve head tissue. The link survived in the team's best statistical model, which also included sex. Cornea and nerve head are far apart in the eye, so a shared trait, perhaps the stiffness of connective tissue throughout the eye, may drive both. If so, a quick cornea test could hint at circulation deeper in the eye.
plos-pone-0351837:
Eline Kroeze and four colleagues trace what care costs in the six months around a stay in Dutch short-term residential care, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. This care is meant to return older patients home independent, yet fewer than half manage it. National claims for more than sixteen thousand patients admitted in 2022 were sorted into cost paths, with a palliative group set aside in advance.

One latent group of about a fifth of patients consumed nearly two fifths of all spending, driven by hospital returns and nursing home admission. Dementia and several diagnoses raised the odds of belonging, but prediction overall was weak. The authors conclude the variation lives in how care is organised, not who the patients are.
plos-pone-0351937:
Diogo Mochcovitch and colleagues present a case study of a training workshop that spread through Quebec primary care largely on its own. The workshop, called STAT-C, teaches family doctors and nurses how to handle sick leave tied to common mental health problems. The team followed its spread for a year after it was showcased at an innovation meeting.

They gathered documents, sat in on monthly meetings, and interviewed the workshop's creators, clinicians, decision makers, and end users. The workshop met most of the checklist points used to judge whether an idea is ready to grow. Interview accounts covered why sites picked it up and what helped or blocked its spread. Cases like this show how good ideas can travel without a central push.
plos-pone-0352137:
Cassandra Barber and four co-authors address a quiet problem in cattle research in this 2026 PLOS ONE article. Lab tests that measure gene activity need steady reference genes for comparison, yet the usual choices may shift between tissues or animals. The team hunted for better candidates in the breathing and immune tissues of cattle.

Starting from dozens of public gene datasets from healthy cattle, they ranked genes by how little their activity varied. Five candidates emerged, and lab tests on tissue from calves infected with a respiratory virus confirmed one gene as steady in most tissues checked. Reliable reference genes make later studies of cattle lung disease far more trustworthy.
plos-pone-0352237:
Yun Song and three colleagues trace how shocks ripple between farm, energy, and money markets under Chinese policy uncertainty. Their 2026 study connects four series: agricultural futures, crude oil, the US dollar, and an index of China's economic policy uncertainty. Average spillovers can hide the real action. The authors therefore use a quantile method that watches calm periods and extremes separately. Crises, in this design, get their own measurement rather than blurring into the mean.

The extremes dominated. Return spillovers at the tails ran far higher than at typical levels. Bad times plainly wire the markets tighter together. Specific crises visibly amplified the transmission. Policy uncertainty itself behaved as part of the system, not background noise. For traders and regulators, the lesson is to watch the tails. Diversification that looks safe in normal months can evaporate exactly when a policy shock hits all three markets at once.
plos-pone-0352337:
Giuliana Nardacchione, Pierluigi Zoccolotti, and Chiara Valeria Marinelli published this 2026 study testing a popular theory of dyslexia. The procedural hypothesis blames weak rule-learning memory. Thirty-two young adults with dyslexia and sixty controls learned an artificial grammar, and the task was split apart to see which kind of learning each person used.

Adults with dyslexia learned the grammar rules and statistical patterns about as well as controls, using stored examples too, though forming those examples was harder. Nardacchione finds little support for the procedural theory and highlights strengths dyslexic adults use to compensate.
plos-pone-0352437:
Marta Majewska and seven colleagues profile the blood chemistry of COVID-19 at four depths of severity. Their 2026 study drew plasma from twenty patients and five healthy controls. Patients were classed by lung involvement and the breathing support they needed. A broad, untargeted scan detected over five hundred metabolites per sample. The team then asked how the chemical picture morphs as the disease deepens, rather than comparing sick and healthy in one lump.

Severity rewired metabolism step by step. The chemical distance from healthy grew steadily across the groups. Early and moderate disease centred on disturbed fatty acid handling. The severest group shifted toward pyrimidine metabolism, the chemistry of building DNA letters. That fits frantic virus replication and immune cell multiplication. One amino acid pathway stayed disturbed across nearly all stages. Fine-grained staging like this could eventually match treatments to the metabolic phase a patient is actually in.
plos-pone-0352937:
Liangliang Jiang and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One remote-sensing study of how Central Asia's vegetation withstands and recovers from drought, season by season. Western Central Asia suffers frequent spring droughts, while the Aral Sea basin gets fewer but harsher summer and autumn droughts. The team measured two qualities: resistance during drought and resilience afterward, across croplands, grasslands, forests, and sparse vegetation.

Croplands in northern Kazakhstan tended to bend but bounce back, while sparse lands downstream of the Aral Sea resisted yet recovered poorly. Rainfall and dryness of the air together drove over half of the variation in resilience. Spring vegetation was both toughest and quickest to recover, and spring also accounted for the largest share of vegetation loss. Long summer droughts hit grasslands hardest. The authors say seasonal detail like this sharpens drought planning.
plos-pone-0353137: Fan, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on safe ways to test tax-risk software. Real tax records are private, so Fan built a simulation that makes fake but realistic data. Rules check that the fake data obey set limits, and the setup can be rerun the same way each time. Shared test data of this kind let tax offices and researchers compare detection tools fairly.
plos-pone-0353237:
Yulin Li and three co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of a simple blood ratio in critically ill bowel disease patients. The ratio compares hemoglobin with the spread of red cell sizes. It tracks inflammation in the body. The data covered an unusual subgroup. These were intensive care patients with bowel disease who all died within thirty days. The question was whether the ratio related to sepsis during the stay.

Patients who developed sepsis had lower ratios on arrival. Each step up in the ratio came with notably lower odds of sepsis. The pattern was steady and straight-line. The authors are candid about the limits. This hand-picked subgroup cannot speak for patients in general. They frame the result as a hypothesis about end-stage bowel disease. Future studies in broader groups should test it.
plos-pone-0353837:
Zeyu Zhang and three colleagues develop a questionnaire for gauging how ready trainee teachers in China are for artificial intelligence, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Five hundred and twenty-eight pre-service teachers answered the draft survey, which the team split into halves to discover and then confirm its structure. The finished tool has fourteen items across three themes: how well teachers understand AI, how risky they judge it, and how confident they feel academically.

Statistical checks showed the three-part structure fit well and each theme measured consistently. Trainees who had already used AI scored higher on literacy and confidence, but slightly lower on caution. Teacher educators now have a tested yardstick for a fast-moving part of training.
plos-pone-0354037:
Henry Mensah and three colleagues soak cowpea seeds in a mutation-causing chemical to breed better varieties, in this 2026 PLOS ONE experiment. Cowpea is a staple protein crop in West Africa, and creating fresh genetic variety is the first step in improving it. Seeds of one cultivar were treated at three strengths of the chemical, grown out, and scored for flowering, pod, seed, and yield traits.

Counter to expectations, germination and survival rose with the chemical dose. The lowest dose gave the best average yield, and two standout plants produced roughly double the control's harvest. Those two mutants advance to the next generation of trials, where their advantage must prove stable and heritable.
plos-pone-0354137:
Krokovsky and colleagues, in a 2026 laboratory study, ask what happens when two mosquito-borne viruses infect the same cells. Zika, West Nile, and Mayaro viruses now overlap in parts of the world, thanks to trade, travel, and a warming climate. A mosquito or a person could carry two at once, or catch one after another.

The team infected monkey kidney cells with Zika plus West Nile, or Zika plus Mayaro, either together or one after the other. When the viruses arrived together, Zika's output fell, a pattern called interference. When Zika arrived first, it held its ground. When Zika arrived second, it was shut out. The partner viruses, by contrast, grew just as well whether Zika was present or not. Six days after infection, the team measured viral RNA and cell damage. The authors frame these dish results as a first step toward understanding double infections in real hosts.
plos-pone-0354237:
Yevusiak and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a trial called REST, about stopping the weight-loss drug semaglutide. The drug helps many people with obesity lose a large amount of weight and improves heart and metabolic health. Yet most people regain weight after stopping suddenly, and the health gains fade.

The trial will enroll people who have already lost at least a tenth of their body weight on the drug and whose weight has leveled off. Half will taper the dose slowly over sixteen weeks before stopping, and half will stop at once. The main measure is how much weight each group regains. Blood pressure across a full day and levels of a hunger hormone will also be tracked. The team expects that a slow taper will soften regain. Their design speaks to a common real-world problem: how to come off a drug many patients cannot take forever.
plos-pone-0354337:
Wei and colleagues, in a 2026 study, model how blue honeysuckle branches shake when a harvest machine vibrates them. Mechanical shaking can knock ripe berries loose, but the trunk and roots soak up much of the energy, weakening the force at the fruit. The team simplified a forked branch into a Y shape and wrote the equations of its motion.

Their math shows that when the branch sits at a small angle to the shaking direction, a certain shaking speed can trigger parametric resonance. That is a runaway wobble that could shake fruit free or, if uncontrolled, harm the branch. The unstable zone depends on shaking strength, speed, and branch size. Computer models of the branch and real shaking tests on branches matched the theory well. The authors offer the model as a design basis for honeysuckle harvesters that shake hard enough to pick, but not to damage.
plos-pone-0354737:

Both local tests found slightly more positives than the reference and agreed with it closely on counts across virus subtypes. Small average biases stayed within a narrow range. The authors say the local tests meet needed standards while costing less and returning results faster, helping close a monitoring gap where resources are tight.
plos-pone-0354837:

plos-pone-0354937:

Researchers often read a tumor's pattern of gene activity as a signature of some process, here glutaminolysis, the cell's use of the amino acid glutamine. The authors show that when PTEN is deleted, neighboring genes are often deleted along with it, as passengers.

Those passenger deletions can distort the signature, making it look as if glutamine use changed when the true cause sits nearby in the genome. Their case argues for location aware signature design: checking what else a deletion drags with it. The lesson reaches beyond one gene, to any study that reads meaning into cancer's copy number changes.
plos-pone-0355437:
Xiaomin Lin and Xudong Huang examine in 2026 whether a simple index built from blood sugar and blood fat relates to early kidney damage in a very large Chinese sample. The damage sign is a raised level of a protein in urine. Tens of thousands of adults from eight centres were included, with many health factors accounted for in the models.

Higher index values linked steadily to higher odds of the urine sign, in a straight line pattern. The link held for people with and without diabetes, but was stronger where diabetes was present. Because the data are a single snapshot, the authors say follow up studies must show whether the index comes before damage.
plos-pone-0355737:
Giulia Tomasetig and seven colleagues scan the brains of professional artists as they judge their own paintings, in this 2026 study. Twenty artists rated artworks by themselves and by others inside an MRI scanner, and in a second task they mentally relived the moment they had conceived each of their pieces. The design tests whether the physical act of making art stays embedded in how its maker later experiences it.

Judging their own work, compared with others', engaged brain regions tied to action and to the emotional feel of movement. Reliving creation recruited a network involved in motor thinking. Artists who showed stronger activity in a movement-planning region during that reliving also judged their works more favorably. The authors read this as support for an embodied view: for painters, the gestures of creation remain part of the finished artwork's experience.
plos-pone-0355937:
Jianfan Zhou and colleagues test whether two simple blood-based scores can flag adults at risk of poor mental health. One score mixes blood sugar and fat measures, and the other compares two blood cell types tied to inflammation. Several hundred adults at a hospital in Shandong, China, completed a standard symptom checklist and gave fasting blood samples for both scores.

Higher values on either score tracked with higher symptom totals across most areas, including low mood, anxiety, and body complaints. Adults high on both scores fared worst. Among several machine learning models, a regularized regression sorted risk best, though modestly. Zhou and colleagues suggest routine blood scores could help flag patients who deserve a closer mental health check.
plos-pone-0356237:
Suzanne Ablard and seven colleagues evaluate community hubs designed to keep urgent-care patients out of hospital in England, in this 2026 qualitative study. The hubs help paramedics and other clinicians route people with pressing but non-emergency needs into nearby community services instead of an ambulance trip. The team interviewed twenty-one staff working in, or referring into, hubs at three locations and analyzed the conversations thematically.

Staff said the hubs genuinely improved integrated working, giving clinicians rapid access to community support for patients. But three brakes limited their impact. Fuzzy eligibility rules created a tension between easy access and consistent decisions. Ambulance services engaged unevenly. And hiring and keeping staff with the right skill mix proved hard. The authors conclude the model can simplify access and prevent needless hospital trips if referral processes, ambulance buy-in, and workforce planning are fixed.
plos-pone-0356837:

Feature picking cuts noise and cost in machine learning, but common tools can flatten the hidden shape of a dataset. Their method uses a curvature-aware penalty to keep complex shapes intact, a compression step to drop repeated features, and a filter that resists stray outliers.

Across nine standard test datasets, the method chose feature sets that performed better than rival approaches, and the team proves their solving routine settles properly. Zhang and colleagues aim the tool at tasks such as image and gene analysis. Those datasets are wide, messy, and unlabeled. Keeping true structure matters more than raw size.
plos-pone-0357037:

Their 2026 study scanned the animals after eight weeks with a technique that measures both tissue thickness and blood flow without contact, comparing them against normally sighted controls.

The myopic eyes were longer, as expected, but also showed thinner choroid and retinal layers and reduced blood flow in the inner retina, differences clear at most measurement points. Those three changes mirror what doctors fear in severe human myopia, where stretched, underfed tissue can tear or degenerate. The imaging markers give researchers a way to track candidate treatments in animals over time.
plos-pone-0357737:

Using a national sample of older adults, they analyzed just over five hundred people needing help with everyday activities. Care networks were sorted by who helped: spouses, children, extended family, friends and neighbors, paid carers, or public services.

Five network types emerged, the largest centered on children and the smallest on friends and neighbors. Compared with child-centered care, people whose networks centered on public services, and those with mixed networks, scored higher on depression, even after adjustments. Pairwise tests showed the same two types also exceeded spouse-centered and friend-centered networks. The overall shape of a care network, not just its size, relates to mental health, they conclude, so assessments should map the whole configuration.
plos-pone-0357837:

plos-pone-0358137:

At the Nandipur plant, three large turbines ran at full load for a year while the team logged output against temperature, humidity, and dew point. Hot air is thinner, so turbines swallow less of it, and operators need forecasts that price the weather in rather than discovering shortfalls at peak demand.

Ambient temperature dominated: as it climbed, output and efficiency fell in a strong, tight relationship. Humidity and dew point mattered too, but more weakly. The team built prediction models three ways, classical regression and two machine learning methods, and validated them on operating data. Their best models give plant managers a practical tool for scheduling generation and maintenance around Pakistan's summers, and for estimating the fuel and emissions cost of each hot day.
plos-pone-0358337:

plos-pone-0358537:

Using field records from 2017 to 2025, the team hunted season specific hotspots separately for the rainfed and irrigated growing seasons, with clustering statistics and interpolation methods.

One subdistrict, Nangalkot, burned as a hotspot in both seasons. Rainfed season severity there averaged roughly half the crop's potential damage range, while irrigated season peaks in several subdistricts ran higher still. The resolution voices disappointment at the lack of progress in the Conference on Disarmament. It builds the case, ahead of the 2015 review conference, that disarmament pledges were overdue.
un-sc-res-1037:
Croatia came before the Security Council in Resolution 1037, adopted on 15 January 1996. Croatia and the local Serb community had signed the Basic Agreement in November 1995. It covered Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Sirmium. Those lands were to return to Croatian rule in peace.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council creates a transitional administration, UNTAES, for twelve months. Up to 5,000 troops will oversee demilitarization within thirty days of full deployment. Civilian staff will build a temporary police force, run services, and organize elections. They will also watch rights, clear mines, and help refugees return. Member states may use close air support to defend the mission if asked.
un-sc-res-1337: Within the United Nations official record, Resolution 1337 is the Security Council text catalogued for 1973. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-137: Judge Sir Hersch Lauterpacht died in May 1960. His death left a vacancy on the International Court of Justice. On 31 May 1960 the Security Council set the election to fill the seat. The vote would take place during the General Assembly's fifteenth session. The decision was adopted without a vote. The short text follows the standard form under the court's statute. It performs that single scheduling act.
un-sc-res-1437:
The Prevlaka observer mission was given its last extension by the Security Council on 11 October 2002. The United Nations Mission of Observers in Prevlaka watched the demilitarized peninsula claimed by Croatia and Yugoslavia. The area had stayed stable and calm. Both sides were making progress in normalizing their relations, including talks on a transitional arrangement for the peninsula.

The Council authorized UNMOP to keep monitoring the demilitarization to 15 December 2002, calling it the last extension of the mandate. The Secretary-General was told to prepare the mission's end by drawing down its staff in stages. The parties had to respect the demilitarized regime and cooperate fully with the observers. The Council welcomed the warming ties between Zagreb and Belgrade. It kept open the option of ending the mission even sooner if the two governments settled the Prevlaka question themselves.
un-sc-res-1537: Resolution 1537, adopted in 2004, is part of the Security Council's continuous numbered record. The collection holds it as a Wikisource transcription of the official UN text. Its paragraphs move from the situation the Council faced to the steps it ordered, the standard path by which a debate in New York becomes action elsewhere.
un-sc-res-1637: Under number 1637, a formal decision of the Security Council is preserved in the record wording from English Wikisource. Resolutions bind together fifteen national positions into one voice, which is why their phrasing is so measured. The entry keeps that measured phrasing entire, letting readers hear the institution speak in its own register.
un-sc-res-1737:
The Security Council turned to Iran's nuclear program in Resolution 1737, adopted on 23 December 2006. United Nations inspectors still could not confirm that the program was purely peaceful. Iran had refused to halt uranium enrichment work as demanded that July. Gaps in knowledge about hidden material and past work stayed open.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council orders Iran to suspend enrichment, reprocessing, and heavy water projects at once. All states must block sales of goods that could feed those programs or missile work. Assets of listed people and firms tied to the program are frozen. A sanctions committee will track compliance. The vote was unanimous, the first sanctions round in a long standoff.
un-sc-res-1937: Security Council Resolution 1937 is held here as a transcription of the official record, sourced from English Wikisource. Its place in the numbered series is its identity in UN citation. The text at that place is complete: the members' stated grounds first, then the operative decisions through which the Council exercised its peace and security powers.
un-sc-res-2337:
Council members took up the Gambia and adopted Resolution 2337 on the Gambia on 19 January 2017. Adama Barrow had won the presidential election held on 1 December 2016. Yahya Jammeh first accepted the result, then rejected it days later. Soldiers seized the election office, and parliament tried to stretch Jammeh's term by three months.

The Council backs the African Union and the West African bloc, ECOWAS, in standing by the election result. It calls on Jammeh to hand power to Barrow by 19 January 2017, as the constitution requires. Gambian soldiers are told to stay calm and serve the elected government. The text matters because regional pressure, backed by the Council, forced a peaceful handover days later.
un-sc-res-237:
Days after the June 1967 war, the Council turned to the people caught in it. On 14 June 1967 it stressed the need to spare civilians and prisoners of war. It said basic human rights must hold even in war. It pointed to the Geneva Conventions of 1949. Those rules govern the treatment of prisoners and the protection of civilians.

The Council called on Israel to guard the safety of people in the areas it had taken. It asked Israel to help those who had fled to return home. It urged all governments in the conflict to respect the Geneva rules in full. The Secretary-General had to track compliance and report back.
un-sc-res-337:
Israeli jets forced down a civilian airliner over Lebanon in August 1973. The plane was Lebanese, leased to Iraqi Airways. Lebanon charged that the seizure broke its sovereignty and threatened civil aviation. On 15 August 1973 the Security Council condemned Israel's act. It found the diversion and seizure violated Lebanon's land and airspace. The act also broke the 1949 armistice and the aviation conventions, the Council said.

The world aviation body was told to weigh this ruling in its safety work. Israel had to stop all such acts at once. If they were repeated, the Council warned, it would consider fitting steps. The vote was unanimous. The incident remains a landmark case on the protection of civil aircraft.
un-sc-res-37: Rules for judging new members were written into the Security Council's own book by Resolution 37, passed on 9 December 1947. A state that seeks a UN seat must send its bid to the Secretary-General. The bid must hold a formal pledge that the state accepts the duties of the Charter. Rule 60 then states the Council's task: judge if the state is peace-loving, and fit and willing to keep those duties, and rule if its bid should be backed.
un-sc-res-837:
Attacks on United Nations troops in Mogadishu drew an armed response order on 6 June 1993. Forces of the United Somali Congress and Somali National Alliance had ambushed UNOSOM II staff on 5 June. Pakistani peacekeepers were among the dead. Radio broadcasts by the alliance had incited the attacks. The Council voiced outrage at the loss of life.

The Council strongly condemned the unprovoked attacks, which it saw as part of a planned drive against the operation. Condolences went to Pakistan and to the families of the fallen. Speed in disarming all Somali parties was again named crucial. The Council restated that the Secretary-General held authority under resolution 814 (1993) to take all necessary measures against those responsible. He was asked to inquire into the incident urgently, above all into the part played by the faction leaders involved. The full and rapid deployment of UNOSOM II's 18,000 troops was urged.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Eastern Slavonia is placed under UN administration by Resolution 1037, adopted on 15 January 1996. The Basic Agreement of 12 November 1995 between Croatia and the local Serb community provided for the region's peaceful reintegration into Croatia. The Secretary-General's December 1995 report set out the operation's design, and the Council stressed human rights for all residents.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council establishes the UN Transitional Administration for Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Sirmium, UNTAES, for an initial 12 months. A Transitional Administrator holds overall authority. The military component, up to 5,000 troops, supervises demilitarization, to be completed within 30 days once the force is ready, and monitors refugee returns. The civilian component builds a temporary police force, runs civil administration and public services, and organizes and certifies elections. Member states may provide close air support in UNTAES's defence.

Lebanon's long-running peacekeeping force, UNIFIL, comes up for renewal on 30 January 2001, at the Lebanese government's request. By then the Council accepted that Israel had pulled its forces out of Lebanon in line with resolution 425, the 1978 text that set the force's core task. What remained was keeping the south calm and helping Lebanon's own authority return.

UNIFIL's mandate was renewed for six months, until 31 July 2001, and its troop numbers were to return to the planned working level by that date. Lebanon was called on to send more of its own soldiers south. Both sides were told to respect the withdrawal line and avoid violence.

This file sits in the Year of Africa, yet its topic is a court seat. Judge Sir Hersch Lauterpacht died on 8 May 1960. He was a famed mind in world law, based in Britain. His death left a gap on the world court bench. Resolution 137 passed without a vote on 31 May 1960.

The Council set the cure for the fall. A ballot would be held at the Assembly's fifteenth session. Both big bodies vote on judges at the same time. The winner would serve just the rest of Lauterpacht's term. His books on law and human rights still shape the field. The text is a brief act of respect, mixed with the plain need to keep the court at full strength.

Resolution 1437 passed by a full vote on 11 October 2002. It winds down a small UN watch team on Croatia's Prevlaka cape. Watchers had kept an eye on this bare strip of land near Dubrovnik since the wars of the 1990s. A UN report that month called the area calm and still.

Croatia and Yugoslavia were mending ties, which the Council cheered. It stretched the team's term one last time, to mid-January 2003. The two states had pledged in 1992 to keep the cape free of troops. A 1996 pact then set their ties on a normal path. Prevlaka was a quiet win for the region, and this text closed the UN file.

Sierra Leone's mission, UNAMSIL, is extended until 30 September 2004 in this text of 30 March 2004. The mission had made good progress toward the benchmarks for winding down. Still, the gains were fragile, above all in the weak state of Sierra Leone's police and armed forces.

The government is urged to build an effective police force, army, prison system, and independent judiciary fast enough to take over law and order from the mission. Stronger control over diamond mining is also demanded. Donors and the mission are encouraged to keep helping, and the Mano River Union states are pressed to resume dialogue for regional peace.

The multinational force in Iraq and the oil-revenue arrangements that support the state are extended on 8 November 2005. Iraq was entering a new phase of its transition. Ahead lay the day Iraqi forces would take full charge of security, and the country's Transitional Government was committed, the text notes, to a federal and democratic country.

The force's mandate is extended, with a review at Iraq's request or by 15 June 2006 at the latest, and an earlier end if Iraq's government asked. The rules channelling oil income into the Development Fund for Iraq under world monitoring are extended until 31 December 2006. The United States is to keep reporting on the force's work on behalf of its member states.

Iran's nuclear programme draws its first Council sanctions in Resolution 1737, adopted on 23 December 2006. The IAEA could not confirm the absence of undeclared nuclear material or activities. Iran had ignored Resolution 1696 (2006). It refused to suspend enrichment-related and reprocessing work. It also refused to cooperate under the Additional Protocol. Six states and the EU were still pressing for a negotiated solution.

Acting under Article 41 of Chapter VII, the Council orders Iran to suspend all enrichment-related and reprocessing activities and heavy-water projects, verified by the IAEA. All states must block supplies of listed proliferation-sensitive items and nuclear-weapon delivery technology. They must stop related technical and financial assistance. They must freeze the assets of the persons and entities named in the resolution's annex. States must also notify a new sanctions Committee of listed persons' travel. The measures are framed to pressure compliance while leaving a diplomatic path open.

Lebanon asked for another year of the United Nations force in its south, and the Council agreed on 30 August 2010. Resolution 1937 concerns UNIFIL, the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon. UNIFIL patrols the area along the Blue Line, the marked border line with Israel. Lebanon's foreign minister had written to request the extension.

The Council extended UNIFIL's mandate until 31 August 2011, without changes. It voiced deep concern about breaches of the 2006 cease-fire terms. A serious clash along the Blue Line on 3 August 2010 was named in particular, and the Council awaited the force's report on it. All sides were pressed to respect the Blue Line. The text also backed the ban on arms outside state control, and it urged Lebanon's armed forces to take on more duties in the south.

The Gambia's election crisis is addressed by Resolution 2337, adopted on 19 January 2017, the day the term was to change hands. Adama Barrow won the 1 December 2016 election. The result was first accepted by the incumbent, Yahya Jammeh. He then rejected it, seized the electoral commission through the army, and declared a state of emergency. ECOWAS and the African Union stood by the result.

The Council urges all Gambian parties to respect the will of the people and endorses the ECOWAS and African Union decisions recognizing Barrow as President. It requests Jammeh to carry out a peaceful transition and transfer power to Barrow by 19 January 2017, as the constitution requires. It gives full support to ECOWAS action, by political means first. Gambian security forces are told to show maximum restraint and place themselves at the disposal of the elected authorities. An update is due within ten days.

Resolution 237 is a UN Security Council humanitarian appeal issued just after the Six-Day War, adopted unanimously on 14 June 1967. The Council cited the urgent need to spare civilians and prisoners of war further suffering and held that basic human rights must be respected even in war.

The resolution calls on Israel to keep the people of the fought-over areas safe, well, and secure, and to let those who fled return home. It recommends all governments concerned follow the Geneva Conventions on prisoners and civilians scrupulously, and asks the Secretary-General to track implementation. It became a reference point for later arguments over the occupied territories' population.

Israeli jets forced down a civil airliner in August 1973. The plane was Lebanese, leased to Iraqi Airways. It had just left Beirut's skies. Lebanon cried foul at once, in a note to the Council. Both sides were heard. Resolution 337 passed with no dissent on 15 August 1973.

Israel was damned by name for the act. The grab broke Lebanon's rule over its soil, the text says. It broke the 1949 armistice and the 1967 ceasefire texts. It broke the rules that guard civil flight as well. The world air body was asked to weigh the case. Israel got a grave charge: shun all such acts, or face steps to force the Council's word. Lives of crew and guests had been put at risk for a hunt that missed its quarry.

Rules for how states join the United Nations were written into the Council's rule book on 9 December 1947. Resolution 37 adds revised rules on admission of new members to the Council's rules of procedure. A state that wants to join applies to the Secretary-General, with a formal declaration that it accepts the obligations of the Charter. The Council then decides whether the applicant is a peace-loving state, able and willing to carry out those obligations. It forwards a recommendation, or a special report, to the General Assembly.

Uzbekistan's seat at the UN began with this line of 1992. On 29 January, the Council adopted Resolution 737 without a vote. The Republic of Uzbekistan had claimed freedom as the Soviet Union broke apart. That break came at the end of 1991. The new state now sought its own place in the world body.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Uzbekistan. The Assembly did so in March 1992. The bid was one of a swift series that winter and spring. Each former Soviet republic turned itself into a sovereign UN member state. The map of Central Asia took its modern shape in those months.

Resolution 837, adopted on 6 June 1993, answers the ambush that killed Pakistani peacekeepers in Mogadishu the day before. Forces linked to the United Somali Congress had launched premeditated attacks on UNOSOM II personnel. The Council expressed outrage at the loss of life and said such acts directly undermined the effort to restore peace and normal life in Somalia.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council reaffirmed that those responsible for the attacks would be held individually accountable. It authorized the UN operation to take all necessary measures against them, including arrest and detention for prosecution, and demanded that all Somali factions stop attacks on UN and relief personnel. The manhunt that followed reshaped the whole intervention.
wilkinson-manners-customs-ancient-egypti:
John Gardner Wilkinson built the first full English tale of old Egypt in Vol. 1 of Manners and Customs of the Ancient Egyptians, out in 1837. Wilkinson had lived in Egypt for years, drawn its walls, and read its script. Most books then gave kings and wars. He gives homes, dress, food, games, and work: life as it was lived each day.

His draws fill the tome with true scenes. The work taught a whole age how that lost world felt at close hand. All books of its kind since owe it a debt. This tome starts the set.

John Gardner Wilkinson turns to the state in Vol. 2 of Manners and Customs of the Ancient Egyptians, out in 1837. The first tome gave the home life of the land. Here come kings, courts, laws, troops, trade, and the work of priests and clerks. Wilkinson draws on walls he had drawn and texts he could read at first hand in Egypt.

His aim is a whole world, not just its kings. Farms, boats, and pay rolls sit by wars and crowns. The tome is the frame that holds the set's home scenes. It shows a state at work.

John Gardner Wilkinson ends his great survey with faith and art in Vol. 3 of Manners and Customs of the Ancient Egyptians, out in 1837. Gods, rites, death, and the tomb fill the first half. The next half turns to paint, carve work, build craft, and the tools of each trade in the land of the Nile in its prime.

Wilkinson writes as one who dwelt there and drew all he saw. The set as a whole founds the theme in English. No work of its age gives so full a world. This tome crowns it with the soul's side.
